name: Murujuga rock art
dateLabel: engravings from c. 45,000 years ago onward
evidenceNote: The carvings have no writing; their great age is estimated from weathering of the rock and from dated sites nearby, and the oldest dates are still being refined.
summary: Murujuga, on the Burrup Peninsula of Western Australia, holds what is described as the world's largest collection of rock engravings: around a million petroglyphs at some 2,500 archaeological sites, alongside quarries and shell middens. Some carvings are thought to be more than 40,000 years old, and Aboriginal people kept adding to them over thousands of years, so the site spans the whole period of this atlas. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in July 2025. Its traditional owners are Aboriginal nations including the Yaburara, and industrial development nearby remains a matter of debate.

name: Apollo 11 Cave
dateLabel: painted slabs c. 28,000 BCE (about 30,000 years old)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the painted stones are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal from the layers they lay in.
summary: A rock shelter in the far south of Namibia, named by its German excavator, Wolfgang Erich Wendt, after the Apollo 11 Moon mission, which had just returned to Earth. Seven loose quartzite slabs painted with animals, including a zebra-like animal and a creature that mixes antelope and cat, were found in layers about 30,000 years old. They are the oldest figurative art known in Africa. People used the shelter on and off for tens of thousands of years, long before farming or writing.

name: Shum Laka
dateLabel: used from c. 30,000 years ago to c. 400 years ago; burials c. 6000 and 1000 BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the layers and burials are dated by radiocarbon, and ancient DNA was read from four children in 2020.
summary: A large rock shelter behind a waterfall in a volcanic crater near Bamenda, in the Grassfields of northwestern Cameroon, the region where Bantu languages probably began. People used it on and off for some 30,000 years. Eighteen skeletons were buried here in two phases, about 8,000 and 3,000 years ago. DNA from four children, the first ancient DNA from West or Central Africa, showed they were related more to Central African hunter-gatherers than to today's Bantu-speaking peoples.

sources.title: Royal Museum for Central Africa: First ancient DNA from West/Central Africa (Shum Laka)

name: Xianrendong Cave
dateLabel: pottery c. 18,000 BCE (20,000–19,000 years ago); used to c. 8000 BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the age of the pottery comes from radiocarbon dates on the soil layers around the sherds, published in Science in 2012.
summary: Xianrendong is a small limestone cave in Wannian County, Jiangxi, which together with the nearby Diaotonghuan rock shelter has produced the oldest pottery yet known anywhere in the world. A 2012 study dated the earliest sherds to 20,000–19,000 years ago, near the end of the last Ice Age. Many fragments carry scorch marks, so the pots were probably used for cooking. They were made by mobile hunter-gatherers thousands of years before farming began, which overturned the old idea that pottery came only after agriculture. Later layers hold evidence of wild and then cultivated rice.

image.caption: Entrance to Xianrendong Cave, Wannian, Jiangxi

name: Monte Verde
dateLabel: c. 12,500 BCE (about 14,500 years ago) — date now challenged
evidenceNote: Most archaeologists accepted the 14,500-year-old date for decades, but a 2026 study argued the camp is under 8,200 years old, and the original team disputes that.
summary: A campsite beside a creek in southern Chile, sealed under peat that preserved wood, rope, animal skin, seaweed, nuts and the bones of an extinct elephant relative. Dated by its excavators to about 14,500 years ago, it became the best-known evidence that people reached South America before the Clovis hunters of North America, overturning the old 'Clovis first' idea. An older layer claimed at about 18,500 years has never been widely accepted, and in 2026 a new study questioned the main date as well.

image.caption: The Monte Verde area in southern Chile in 2012

name: Huaca Prieta
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the mound's layers are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal, plants and shell.
summary: A huge dark mound of ash, stone, shells, plant remains and textiles on the Pacific shore of the Chicama Valley in northern Peru, inside the El Brujo complex. People camped here as early as about 14,500 years ago and kept living and building on the spot for thousands of years before pottery arrived. Its people fished, gathered shellfish and grew squash, beans, peppers, gourds and cotton, and the site has given some of the earliest evidence for the use of avocado.

image.caption: Cotton and bast cloth from Huaca Prieta, about 2500 BCE (American Museum of Natural History)

name: ʿAin Mallaha (Eynan)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is known from excavations and radiocarbon dates on bones and charcoal.
summary: A Natufian village of round stone-based huts beside the old Lake Hula in northern Israel. Its people still hunted and gathered wild food, yet they lived here all year round, one of the earliest examples of settled life before farming. They buried their dead under and around the houses. One grave held an elderly person with a hand resting on a puppy, among the oldest evidence for a close bond between people and dogs.

name: Raqefet Cave
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the burials are dated by radiocarbon, and the claim that people brewed beer here is still debated.
summary: A cave on Mount Carmel in Israel used by Natufian foragers as a cemetery. Impressions of stems, leaves and flowers in the mud lining of several graves suggest the dead were laid on beds of flowering plants, the oldest known example of this custom. Stone mortars cut into the cave floor held traces of cereals; one team argued in 2018 that they were used to make a kind of beer, but other scholars think they were for grinding flour.

image.caption: Entrance to Raqefet Cave on Mount Carmel

name: Tell Abu Hureyra
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from a rescue dig in 1972–73 and radiocarbon dates on seeds and bones.
summary: A mound on the Euphrates in Syria that records the switch from foraging to farming in one place. The first village belonged to hunter-gatherers; plant remains suggest they began cultivating rye around 13,000 years ago, possibly the earliest cereal farming known. A later, much larger farming village of mudbrick houses followed. The site was excavated in a hurry before the Tabqa Dam flooded it, and it now lies under Lake Assad.

name: Blackwater Draw (Clovis type site)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the Clovis layer is dated by radiocarbon and by its distinctive stone spear points.
summary: A dry stream channel near Clovis, New Mexico, where in 1929 a local man, Ridgley Whiteman, recognised stone tools lying with the bones of mammoths. Excavations from 1932 showed that hunters had killed or butchered mammoths and other big game here at the end of the Ice Age. The fluted spear points found here gave their name to the Clovis culture, for decades thought to be the first people in the Americas. Later layers hold Folsom points and remains of other periods.

name: Pedra Furada (Serra da Capivara)
dateLabel: rock paintings from c. 10,000 BCE; claimed traces 48,000–32,000 years old disputed
evidenceNote: The paintings and later camps are accepted, but claims that people lived here 48,000–32,000 years ago rest on charcoal and broken stones that many experts think could be natural.
summary: A rock shelter at the heart of Serra da Capivara National Park in northeastern Brazil, part of a group of more than 800 sites with hundreds of rock paintings, some from about 12,000 years ago. Brazilian archaeologist Niède Guidon reported hearths and stone tools dated 48,000–32,000 years old, which would mean people reached the Americas extremely early. That claim is still debated. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Serra da Capivara National Park

name: Spirit Cave
dateLabel: c. 12,000–7,000 radiocarbon years ago (very roughly 10,000–5500 BCE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the occupation layers were dated by radiocarbon in the 1960s and 1970s.
summary: Spirit Cave is a hillside cave in Mae Hong Son Province, northwestern Thailand, excavated by Chester Gorman in the mid-1960s. Hunter-gatherers of the Hoabinhian tradition used it for four short periods between about 12,000 and 7,000 uncalibrated radiocarbon years ago, leaving pebble tools, food remains and later some pottery and polished stone. The site was once presented as early evidence for farming in Southeast Asia, but that claim has since been dropped. It remains a key reference for how forest foragers of mainland Southeast Asia lived after the Ice Age.

name: Tassili n'Ajjer rock art
dateLabel: c. 10,000 BCE (debated) to the early centuries CE
evidenceNote: The paintings are real, but they are very hard to date and scholars disagree by thousands of years about how old the earliest styles are.
summary: A sandstone plateau in the Algerian Sahara holding thousands of rock paintings and engravings made over many millennia, when the Sahara was greener. The styles are grouped in a sequence: early wild animals, the 'Round Head' figures, scenes of cattle herders, and later pictures of horses, chariots and camels. Together they show how life changed as the Sahara dried out. The site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and national park.

name: Jericho (Tell es-Sultan)
dateLabel: c. 10,000 BCE – Persian period; tower and wall c. 8000 BCE
evidenceNote: The Neolithic town is dated by excavation and radiocarbon; excavators found no walled city at the time the Bible's story of Joshua is usually placed.
summary: One of the oldest continuously settled places on Earth, beside a strong spring near the Dead Sea. By about 8000 BCE the farming town was enclosed by a stone wall over 3.6 m high, with an 8.5 m stone tower inside, among the oldest monumental buildings known. Kathleen Kenyon excavated the tower in the 1950s. Later Bronze Age Jericho was destroyed in the 16th century BCE; the Bible's tale of its walls falling is not supported by the excavations.

image.caption: The Neolithic stone tower at Tell es-Sultan (Jericho)

name: Bhimbetka rock shelters
dateLabel: paintings c. 10,000 BCE (Mesolithic) to medieval times; occupation far older
evidenceNote: No writing; the paintings are dated by their style, by what they show and by excavated layers, so their dates are approximate.
summary: More than 750 rock shelters spread over seven sandstone hills in central India. People sheltered here for over 100,000 years, and some 400 shelters hold paintings in red and white. The oldest are put at about 10,000 BCE, in the Mesolithic, and show hunting, dancing and animals such as elephants, deer and bison; later layers add riders on horseback and simple geometric designs from historic times. It is the oldest known rock art in India and one of the largest prehistoric art sites in Asia.

image.caption: Paintings in Rock Shelter 8

name: Karahan Tepe
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site has been dug only since 2019 and its dates come from a small but growing set of radiocarbon samples.
summary: A Stone Age site in Şanlıurfa province, Turkey, about 46 km east of Göbekli Tepe and closely related to it. Builders cut rooms into the bedrock and set up T-shaped pillars; one chamber holds a carved human head emerging from the wall above a row of stone pillars. It belongs to the 'Taş Tepeler' (Stone Hills), a group of about a dozen similar sites now being excavated, which show that Göbekli Tepe was not unique.

image.caption: Carved stone pillars in a rock-cut room at Karahan Tepe

name: Lepenski Vir
evidenceNote: No writing existed; its story comes from excavations begun in the 1960s and from radiocarbon dates, which still leave the start date uncertain.
summary: Lepenski Vir sits on the Danube in the Iron Gates gorge of Serbia. Fishers and hunters lived here for thousands of years. Between about 6300 and 6000 BCE, as the first farmers arrived in the region, they built unusual trapezoid-shaped houses with red lime-plaster floors and carved large boulder sculptures of fish-like human faces. Because the village was planned and lived in all year, some have called it Europe's 'first city', though it was a village of foragers. The remains were moved uphill when a dam flooded the gorge and are shown under a roof.

image.caption: House floors of Lepenski Vir under the protective roof

name: Göbekli Tepe
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything we know comes from excavations since 1995 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A hilltop in southeastern Turkey where people built round enclosures of huge T-shaped limestone pillars, the tallest about 5 m high, about 11,500 years ago, among the oldest known megaliths. Many pillars are carved with foxes, boars, snakes and vultures, and some have arms and belts, suggesting stylised humans. First seen as a temple used by roaming hunters, it is now known to have had houses, cisterns and heavy cereal processing. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Excavated enclosures with T-shaped stone pillars at Göbekli Tepe

name: Ounjougou
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the pottery is dated by radiocarbon and luminescence on the river layers it was found in.
summary: A group of more than 100 sites along the Yamé valley on the Bandiagara Plateau in Mali's Dogon Country. Its layers record tens of thousands of years of changing climate and human life. In deposits dated to at least 9400 BCE, archaeologists found broken pots, the oldest pottery known in Africa. It suggests that people in the then-greener Sahel invented pottery on their own, perhaps to cook wild grains, at roughly the same time as in East Asia and long before farming.

image.caption: Part of the Ounjougou site complex in the Yamé valley

name: Shangshan
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site is dated by radiocarbon on its oldest layers, excavated in 2001–2006.
summary: Shangshan, beside the Puyang River in Pujiang County, Zhejiang, is the type site of the Shangshan culture, with more than 20 related sites in the lower Yangtze region. Its oldest layers, dated about 11,400 to 8,600 years ago, contain house remains, pits, possible burials, stone tools and pottery tempered with rice husks. Studies of the pots suggest people processed acorns, cooked food and may have fermented rice. Shangshan is described as the earliest Holocene site in China where houses, pottery and plant processing all appear together, an early step towards rice farming.

name: Star Carr
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from finds preserved in waterlogged peat show people used the lakeside for about 800 years.
summary: Star Carr in North Yorkshire is the most informative Middle Stone Age (Mesolithic) site in Britain. Hunter-gatherers camped on the shore of a lake soon after the Ice Age, when Britain was still joined to mainland Europe. Because the site lies in wet peat, wood, bone and antler survived. Finds include Britain's oldest known structure, 21 red-deer skull caps that may have been worn as headdresses, and nearly 200 antler points. Radiocarbon dates place the activity between about 9300 and 8500 BCE.

name: Guilá Naquitz Cave
dateLabel: used c. 8800–6900 BCE and again c. 650–1450 CE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon on seeds, rinds and other plant remains from the cave floor.
summary: A small cave in the Oaxaca Valley of southern Mexico used by bands of foragers on short visits. Its dry floor preserved squash seeds and rinds about 10,000 years old, the earliest known evidence for a domesticated crop in the Americas, plus early bottle gourds and beans. Some of the oldest maize cobs ever found came from here too, though maize itself was probably first domesticated elsewhere in Mexico. The cave is part of the Prehistoric Caves of Yagul and Mitla World Heritage Site.

name: Çayönü
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is dated by excavations from 1964 to 1991 and radiocarbon.
summary: An early farming village near Diyarbakır in southeastern Turkey, at the foot of the Taurus Mountains near a tributary of the Tigris. Over two thousand years its people moved from round huts to rectangular houses on stone 'grill' foundations, built special public buildings, and worked copper and malachite. Its people grew emmer and einkorn wheat, and it is a key site for the early domestication of pigs and cattle.

image.caption: The mound of Çayönü below the Taurus foothills

name: Gobero
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon on bones, shells and pottery temper, published in 2008.
summary: An ancient lakeside in the Ténéré Desert of Niger, found in 2000 by a photographer on Paul Sereno's fossil-hunting expedition. About 200 burials lie here, the oldest cemetery known in the Sahara. Two different peoples used it: Kiffian hunter-fishers around 7700–6200 BCE, who caught Nile perch up to 2 metres long with bone harpoons, and, after a dry spell, Tenerean people around 5200–2500 BCE, who also kept some cattle. One grave holds a woman and two children buried with arms entwined.

image.caption: Gobero from the air: low dunes where an ancient lake once lay
image.credit: Paul C. Sereno, Elena A. A. Garcea, Hélène Jousse, Christopher M. Stojanowski, Jean-François Saliège, Abdoulaye Maga, Oumarou A. Ide, Kelly J. Knudson, Anna Maria Mercuri, Thomas W. Stafford, Jr., Thomas G. Kaye, Carlo Giraudi, Isabella Massamba N'siala, Enzo Cocca, Hannah M. Moots, Didier B. Dutheil, Jeffrey P. Stivers

sources.title: Sereno et al. 2008, PLoS ONE: Lakeside cemeteries in the Sahara

name: Pengtoushan
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site is dated by radiocarbon, and its dates vary widely, so the range is approximate.
summary: Pengtoushan, in Li County, northwestern Hunan, was excavated in 1988 and gave its name to the Pengtoushan culture of the middle Yangtze. Rice remains here have been radiocarbon dated to about 8200–7800 BCE, and the grains are larger than wild rice, so they are among the early evidence for rice cultivation in China. The site also produced cord-marked pottery placed in graves. Dating Pengtoushan has been difficult, with results from about 9000 to 5500 BCE, so its exact span is uncertain.

name: Nabta Playa
dateLabel: c. 7500–3500 BCE; stone circle 5th millennium BCE
evidenceNote: The camps, cattle burials and stones are real and dated by radiocarbon, but whether the stone circle was really an astronomical calendar is debated.
summary: A seasonal lake basin in the Egyptian desert about 100 km west of Abu Simbel, visited by herders when the Sahara was wetter. They dug wells, built huts in rows, made early pottery and buried cattle under stone mounds. A small ring of upright stones, the 'calendar circle', and lines of larger stones have been claimed as alignments to the summer solstice and to certain stars; some proposed alignments have been rejected by other researchers.

image.caption: Reconstruction of the Nabta Playa stone circle at the Nubia Museum, Aswan

name: Bhirrana
dateLabel: claimed c. 7500 BCE; most scholars: 4th millennium BCE to c. 1900 BCE
evidenceNote: Two charcoal samples gave dates near 7500 BCE, but they came from layers with pottery and copper dated to around 3500 BCE elsewhere, so many scholars doubt the early date.
summary: A village and town on the dry Ghaggar river in Haryana that grew from an early Hakra Ware settlement of pit dwellings into a walled Harappan town with streets and mudbrick houses. The Archaeological Survey of India reported two very early radiocarbon dates and called it the oldest Indus site. Other samples from the same early levels date to 3200–2600 BCE, and the copper tools fit a later stage, so its early chronology remains contested.

name: Cueva de las Manos
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the paintings are dated by radiocarbon, by the layers they lie above, and by bone paint-blowing pipes found below them.
summary: A cave and rock shelters above the Pinturas River canyon in Patagonia, Argentina, famous for hundreds of stencilled hands, almost all of them left hands, made by blowing paint through bone pipes. Hunter-gatherers painted here in waves over about 8,000 years, also showing guanacos, hunting scenes and symbols. It is one of the best records of the earliest peoples of southern South America and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Stencilled hands on the cave wall

name: ʿAin Ghazal
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village and its statues are dated by excavation and radiocarbon.
summary: A large Neolithic farming town on the edge of modern Amman, Jordan, which around 7000 BCE covered 10–15 hectares and housed perhaps 3,000 people. It is famous for 15 statues and 15 busts of lime plaster built over reed frames, with staring eyes outlined in bitumen, found buried in two pits in 1983 and 1985. Made between about 7200 and 6250 BCE, they are among the oldest large human figures ever found. Many are now in the Jordan Museum.

image.caption: One of the plaster statues from ʿAin Ghazal

name: Çatalhöyük
evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is known from excavations since 1958 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A very large Neolithic town on the Konya Plain in central Turkey, home to several thousand people. Houses were packed so tightly that there were no streets: people walked over the roofs and climbed in through holes. Rooms were decorated with wall paintings, plaster bull heads and horns, and the dead were buried beneath the floors. Houses look much alike, which suggests a fairly equal society. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012.

image.caption: Excavated mudbrick houses under the protective roof at Çatalhöyük

name: Jarmo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is dated by excavations in the 1940s–50s and radiocarbon.
summary: A small farming village in the Zagros foothills of Iraqi Kurdistan, among oak and pistachio woods. Robert Braidwood of the University of Chicago's Oriental Institute excavated it to find where farming began. Its people grew early wheat and barley and kept goats and sheep, living in mud-walled houses. Jarmo showed that the hilly flanks of the Fertile Crescent, not only river valleys, were where agriculture took root.

name: Jiahu
evidenceNote: No readable writing exists; the village is dated by radiocarbon, and whether signs scratched on its shells are an early form of writing is debated.
summary: Jiahu, near Wuyang in Henan, was a moated village of the early Peiligang culture, settled about 7000 BCE and abandoned after a flood around 5700 BCE. It housed perhaps 250–800 people. Jiahu is famous for 33 flutes carved from crane wing bones, among the oldest playable instruments in the world, and for signs scratched on tortoise shells and bones. Some see these 'Jiahu symbols' as early proto-writing, but most scholars think they are only a long tradition of sign use, not writing. Residues suggest an early fermented drink of rice, honey and fruit.

name: Kuk Swamp
dateLabel: drainage from c. 7000 BCE (about 9,000 years ago)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the buried ditches and plant remains were dated by radiocarbon.
summary: Kuk Swamp lies in the Wahgi Valley of the Papua New Guinea highlands, about 1,550 metres above sea level. Excavations found drainage ditches dug from about 9,000 years ago to turn wetland into gardens for taro, and evidence that bananas and sugar cane were cultivated from about 6,900–6,400 years ago. It is one of the few places in the world where people invented farming independently, without borrowing crops from elsewhere. UNESCO listed it in 2008. The Kawelka people farm the area today.

name: Peiligang
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site and its culture are dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
summary: Peiligang, a village site in Xinzheng near Zhengzhou in Henan, was discovered in 1977 and gave its name to the Peiligang culture. Its people grew millet, raised pigs, hunted deer and boar and fished with hemp nets. They made some of the oldest pottery in northern China and used stone sickles and grinding slabs to process grain. Like other Peiligang villages, it had separate areas for houses and for the dead. Archaeologists think these communities were egalitarian, with little sign of chiefs or rich graves.

name: Sesklo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dates come from excavated layers and radiocarbon, and the oldest pre-pottery levels are still debated.
summary: Sesklo, near Volos in Thessaly, gave its name to one of Europe's earliest farming cultures. Its people grew wheat and barley and herded sheep, goats, cattle and pigs. The oldest levels have no pottery, but villagers soon made fine painted ware with red and brown geometric patterns. Houses of mudbrick on stone foundations were laid out with some planning, and a few had two floors. At its peak, around 5000 BCE, the settlement may have covered about 20 hectares, though population estimates of up to 5,000 people are uncertain.

name: Ugarit (Ras Shamra)
dateLabel: c. 7000–1185 BCE; golden age c. 1500–1200 BCE
evidenceNote: Thousands of clay tablets found in the city, in several languages, describe its kings, trade and religion.
summary: A port city on the Syrian coast north of Latakia, settled since the Neolithic. In its golden age, about 1500–1200 BCE, it ruled a small trading kingdom linked to Egypt, Cyprus, the Aegean and the Hittites. Its archives include tablets in a cuneiform alphabet of 30 letters, one of the oldest alphabets known, and myths of the god Baal. The city was destroyed around 1185 BCE during the Late Bronze Age collapse.

name: Mehrgarh
dateLabel: c. 7000 BCE (excavators) or c. 5200 BCE (2025 re-dating) to c. 2600 BCE
evidenceNote: The village is well excavated, but its start date is debated: the excavators put it near 7000 BCE, while 2025 radiocarbon dates on tooth enamel put the first farmers at about 5200 BCE.
summary: A farming village near the Bolan Pass in Balochistan, Pakistan, excavated by a French team from 1974. Its mudbrick houses, graves and granaries show people growing wheat and barley and herding sheep, goats and cattle, the earliest farming known in South Asia. Burials held ornaments of sea shell, turquoise and lapis lazuli brought from far away. Later phases added pottery, copper and bead workshops before the site was left around 2600 BCE for nearby Nausharo, as the Indus cities rose.

image.caption: Excavated mudbrick ruins at Mehrgarh

sources.title: Mutin et al. 2025, Scientific Reports: new radiocarbon dates from Neolithic Mehrgarh (PMC)

name: Starčevo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon results at many Starčevo-culture villages, not just this one.
summary: The village of Starčevo, on the north bank of the Danube opposite Belgrade, is the type site of the Starčevo culture: the first farmers of the central Balkans. These communities came north from Greece and Anatolia, bringing wheat, barley, domestic animals and pottery. They lived in small villages of pit-houses and timber houses along the rivers. Radiocarbon dates from 2020 suggest farming spread up the river valleys of Serbia from about 6200 BCE. Their descendants helped carry farming on into central Europe.

name: Tell Halaf
dateLabel: c. 6100–5400 BCE (Halaf village); later the Aramaean city of Guzana
evidenceNote: The Neolithic village had no writing and is dated by excavation; the later city of Guzana is named in Assyrian texts.
summary: A mound near Ras al-Ayn in northeastern Syria that gave its name to the Halaf culture, famous for finely painted pottery with geometric and animal designs. Max von Oppenheim dug here from 1911, mostly exposing the much later palace of the Aramaean city of Guzana with stone statues and reliefs. Many of those finds were smashed when a Berlin museum was bombed in 1943 and have since been pieced back together.

image.caption: Excavated remains of the northeast palace at Tell Halaf

name: Jeitun
dateLabel: c. 6000 BCE, for a few centuries
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dates come from eleven radiocarbon samples taken in excavations in the 1990s.
summary: The oldest known farming village in Central Asia, in the foothills of the Kopet Dag mountains north of Ashgabat, Turkmenistan. About thirty one-room houses of sun-dried clay blocks, each with a hearth and plastered floor, housed perhaps 150–200 people. They grew barley and wheat and kept goats and sheep, much like the first farmers of Iran. Radiocarbon dates from British–Turkmen excavations show it was settled around 6000 BCE and used for only a few centuries.

sources.title: Harris, Gosden & Charles 1996, Jeitun: recent excavations (Proceedings of the Prehistoric Society)

name: Vinča–Belo Brdo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the Vinča symbols scratched on pots are not considered true writing by most scholars, so dates come from layers and radiocarbon.
summary: Belo Brdo ('White Hill') at Vinča, 14 km downstream from Belgrade, is a tell: a mound about 10 metres high made almost entirely of the remains of settlements built one on top of another. Its main layers belong to the Vinča culture, which is named after it. Vinča farmers made thousands of clay figurines and scratched mysterious signs on pottery, and the culture has some of the earliest known evidence of copper smelting. Excavations began in 1908, and finds are now in museums in Belgrade, Oxford and London.

name: Hemudu
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the waterlogged village was dated by radiocarbon after its discovery in 1973.
summary: Hemudu, about 22 km northwest of Ningbo in Zhejiang, was found in 1973 and is the type site of the Hemudu culture. Waterlogged soil preserved long wooden houses raised on stilts, along with large amounts of rice, bone spades used in the fields, and black pottery. A red lacquered wooden bowl from the culture, dated to about 5000–4000 BCE, is among the earliest lacquerware known. Two major floods affected the settlement. Some scholars suggest the Hemudu people were linked to the ancestors of Austronesian-speaking peoples.

name: Eridu
evidenceNote: The early temples are known from excavation; later Sumerian texts name Eridu and call it the first city.
summary: A mound in southern Iraq that Sumerian tradition remembered as the oldest city, where kingship first came down from heaven. Excavators found eighteen mudbrick temples built one on top of another, beginning with a tiny shrine of the Ubaid period and growing into a large platform temple, which shows how Mesopotamian temples developed over time. The city's god was Enki. The ruins of a ziggurat of Ur-Nammu still stand.

image.caption: Baked bricks of the ziggurat at Eridu

name: Bangudae Petroglyphs
evidenceNote: Rock carvings cannot be radiocarbon dated, so their age is estimated from their style and from finds nearby; the start date is approximate.
summary: The Bangudae petroglyphs are carvings on a cliff beside a tributary of the Taehwa River near Ulsan, South Korea, found in 1970. More than 300 images show whales, deer, tigers, boats and human figures, including some of the earliest known scenes of whale hunting anywhere. The animals are drawn so carefully that many species can be identified, such as a mother grey whale carrying her calf. The main carvings are usually attributed to Neolithic people, with later additions continuing for thousands of years. The site was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2025.

name: Uruk (Eanna and the White Temple)
dateLabel: c. 5000 BCE – c. 700 CE; Eanna and White Temple c. 3500–3100 BCE
evidenceNote: Uruk is where some of the earliest writing was found, and it is named in thousands of later texts.
summary: The great city of southern Iraq that gave its name to the Uruk period. Around 3100 BCE it may have held up to 50,000 people, probably the largest town in the world then. In the Eanna temple district of the goddess Inanna archaeologists found some of the oldest written tablets; the White Temple, whitewashed and set on a high terrace, stood in the Anu district. Later tradition made Gilgamesh a king of Uruk.

image.caption: The Anu ziggurat at Uruk, base of the White Temple

name: Cairn of Barnenez
dateLabel: built c. 4850–4000 BCE; reused in the 3rd millennium BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dating shows the two building phases.
summary: The Cairn of Barnenez in northern Brittany is a long stone mound containing a row of passage-grave chambers; a second phase added six more. Radiocarbon dates put its first phase between about 4850 and 4250 BCE and its second between 4450 and 4000 BCE, making it one of the oldest megalithic monuments in Europe. Some stones are carved with symbols. Pottery shows people reused it in the Bronze Age. In the 1950s part of it was being quarried for paving stone before it was saved and restored.

name: Banpo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is dated by radiocarbon, and the signs painted on its pots are not considered writing.
summary: Banpo, east of Xi'an in the Wei River valley, was discovered in 1953 and is the classic village of the early Yangshao culture. Five to six hectares of round and square houses, many half sunk into the ground with thatched roofs, were surrounded by a ditch about 5–6 metres wide. Pottery kilns and a cemetery lay outside. Banpo is known for its painted red pottery and for simple signs marked on pots, which are not true writing. The Xi'an Banpo Museum, built over the excavation in 1957, shows how a village of millet farmers lived.

name: Budj Bim eel traps
dateLabel: from at least c. 4600 BCE (6,600 years ago)
evidenceNote: The Gunditjmara kept no written records; one eel-trap system has been radiocarbon dated to about 6,600 years ago, and Gunditjmara oral history describes the landscape.
summary: Around the Budj Bim volcano in southwest Victoria, Australia, the Gunditjmara people built channels, weirs and dams in old lava flows to trap short-finned eels and fish. One of the trap systems at Lake Condah has been carbon dated to about 6,600 years old, making it one of the oldest aquaculture systems in the world. Stone house bases nearby suggest settled villages. The Budj Bim Cultural Landscape was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019, and the Gunditjmara still care for it today.

name: Rakhigarhi
dateLabel: village from c. 4600 BCE; city c. 2600–1900 BCE
evidenceNote: The Indus script cannot be read, so the city is known from excavation and radiocarbon dating.
summary: One of the largest Indus cities, on the plain of the Ghaggar river in Haryana. Its mounds span a pre-Harappan village, an early town and a mature city of about 80–100 hectares or more, with planned streets, drains and a cemetery of the mature phase. In 2019 scientists read the first ancient genome from an Indus skeleton, found here; it showed no trace of the steppe ancestry that spread into South Asia later.

image.caption: One of the Rakhigarhi mounds

name: Varna Necropolis
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates published in 2006 show when the graves were dug.
summary: This Copper Age cemetery was found by accident in 1972 by an excavator driver in Varna, Bulgaria. Archaeologists have uncovered 294 graves, some filled with gold ornaments, copper tools, fine flint blades and shells. It holds the oldest large hoard of worked gold in the world. The richest grave, of a man buried with gold regalia, is the oldest known burial of an elite person: an early sign that some people had far more wealth and status than others. Several 'symbolic' graves held no body, only objects and clay masks.

image.caption: A grave from the Varna necropolis with gold ornaments, Varna Archaeological Museum

name: Akrotiri
dateLabel: settled by c. 4500 BCE; buried c. 1600 BCE
evidenceNote: A few Linear A signs survive, but that script is undeciphered, so we rely on excavation; the eruption is dated by radiocarbon to about 1620–1530 BCE, and archaeologists debate the exact date.
summary: Akrotiri on the island of Santorini (Thera) was a busy Bronze Age harbour town with paved streets, drains and houses up to three storeys high. It traded across the Aegean and was closely linked to Minoan Crete. In the 16th century BCE a huge volcanic eruption buried it in ash, preserving it like a Bronze Age Pompeii, with beautiful wall paintings, pottery and furniture. Its ancient name is unknown. Excavation began in 1967, and a roof now covers the ruins.

image.caption: Excavated houses at Akrotiri under the modern roof

name: Carnac stones
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from excavation of the stones and nearby tombs, and exactly when each row was raised is uncertain.
summary: Around Carnac in southern Brittany more than 3,000 standing stones, cut from local granite, stand in long rows, together with stone tombs and burial mounds. It is the largest collection of its kind in the world. They were raised by Stone Age farmers, perhaps from around 4500 BCE, with most work probably around 3300 BCE. Nobody knows for sure what the rows were for. Local legends later said they were Roman soldiers turned to stone.

image.caption: Standing stones of the Le Ménec alignments, Carnac

name: Areni-1 cave
evidenceNote: No writing existed; finds are dated by radiocarbon and kept well by the cave's dry, cool air.
summary: A cave beside the Arpa River in southern Armenia used by Copper Age people for storage, rituals and burials. Its dry air preserved remarkable things: a one-piece leather shoe about 5,500 years old, the oldest leather footwear known, and a winemaking installation of about 4100–4000 BCE, described as the oldest known winery. Burials and storage jars show the cave also had ritual uses.

image.caption: The Arpa River gorge with the Areni-1 cave

name: Susa
evidenceNote: Excavated since the 1850s and named in Elamite, Mesopotamian, Persian and Greek writings.
summary: One of the oldest cities in the world, in Khuzestan, southwestern Iran, between the Karkheh and Dez rivers. It was founded around 4200 BCE, became the capital of Elam, and later served as a capital of the Persian kings, who built a great palace here. The famous law code stele of Hammurabi was found at Susa in 1901, where Elamite raiders had carried it. The modern town of Shush stands on the site.

name: Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dating comes from pottery styles and excavated layers.
summary: The Hypogeum ('underground place') at Paola, Malta, is a maze of chambers cut into solid rock, covering about 500 square metres. It was used as a sanctuary and burial place, and the remains of more than 7,000 people were recorded. Finds included finely decorated pottery and stone and clay figures. Builders found it by accident in 1902 while cutting water cisterns. It is one of the best-preserved works of Malta's temple-building culture.

name: Hierakonpolis (Nekhen)
evidenceNote: The early town is dated by excavation and radiocarbon; writing appears only at the very end, on objects such as the Narmer Palette.
summary: The leading town of Upper Egypt before the pharaohs, about 100 km south of Luxor. Already by 3600 BCE it stretched over 3 km along the Nile, with breweries, potteries, a temple to the falcon god Horus and an elite cemetery. Its 'Painted Tomb' has the oldest known Egyptian tomb painting. The Narmer Palette, which shows a king of about 3100 BCE triumphing over enemies, was found here.

sources.title: Hierakonpolis Expedition: Firsts of the First City

name: Arslantepe
evidenceNote: The early palace had no writing and is dated by radiocarbon; the later city of Melid appears in Hittite and Assyrian texts.
summary: A mound near Malatya in eastern Turkey on a tributary of the Euphrates. Around 3400–3200 BCE it had a mudbrick temple-palace complex with clay sealings for controlling goods, an early example of a state-like administration in contact with Uruk Mesopotamia. In it archaeologists found some of the oldest known swords, made of arsenic bronze. Much later it was a Neo-Hittite city with lion sculptures. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

name: Abydos
evidenceNote: The early royal tombs are known from excavation and early inscriptions; later texts and temples name it as Osiris's holy city.
summary: A sacred site in Upper Egypt whose desert cemetery, Umm el-Qaab, holds the tombs of Egypt's first kings, from before the First Dynasty to the Second. Later Egyptians believed the god Osiris was buried here, and pilgrims came for his festival for thousands of years. The temple of Seti I, built around 1290 BCE, contains the Abydos King List, which names most earlier pharaohs in order.

image.caption: Temple of Seti I at Abydos

name: Sannai-Maruyama
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the settlement is dated by radiocarbon and Jōmon pottery styles, from excavations that began in 1992.
summary: Sannai-Maruyama, in Aomori, northern Japan, was found in 1992 during survey work for a baseball stadium. It turned out to be one of the largest Jōmon settlements, covering about 40 hectares. Hunter-gatherers used the site from about 3900 BCE, and it grew into a long-lived village with longhouses, storage pits, more than 500 burial pits and a great building on six chestnut posts, built around 2600 BCE. Finds include clay figurines, baskets and lacquerware. The village ended around 2300 BCE. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan.

image.caption: Reconstructed six-post tower and longhouse at Sannai-Maruyama

name: Talianki mega-site
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the town was found from the air in the 1970s and dated by excavation, and its population is only an estimate that scholars disagree about.
summary: Near the village of Talianky in central Ukraine lies the largest known settlement of Neolithic Europe, built by the Cucuteni–Trypillia culture. Rings of joined houses, many with two storeys and painted walls, spread over 3 to 4.5 square kilometres of plateau. Estimates of its population range from about 6,000 to more than 15,000 people, which would make it as big as early cities in Mesopotamia. Trypillian settlements usually lasted only 60 to 80 years before their houses were burned, for reasons scholars still debate.

name: Real Alto
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is dated by radiocarbon and by its changing pottery styles.
summary: A village site in the Chanduy valley on the coast of Ecuador, first identified in 1971. It is the best-studied settlement of the Valdivia culture, one of the earliest pottery-making farming peoples in the Americas. By about 2500 BCE perhaps 1,250 people lived here in houses arranged around two plazas with two ceremonial mounds. One of their crops was leren (Calathea allouia), a starchy root.

name: Ur (ziggurat and Royal Cemetery)
dateLabel: c. 3800–500 BCE; Royal Cemetery c. 2600 BCE; ziggurat 21st century BCE
evidenceNote: Ur is named in many cuneiform texts, and its kings left inscriptions on the ziggurat's bricks.
summary: A major Sumerian city in southern Iraq, once near the Persian Gulf coast. Leonard Woolley's digs (1922–34) uncovered the Royal Cemetery of about 2600 BCE, where rulers such as Queen Puabi were buried with gold, lyres, the 'Standard of Ur' and dozens of attendants who died with them. The great ziggurat was built by King Ur-Nammu in the 21st century BCE and restored by Nabonidus about 1,500 years later.

image.caption: The Ziggurat of Ur, with its partly rebuilt facade

name: Dolmen of Menga
evidenceNote: No writing existed; its age comes from excavation and dating of the site.
summary: The Dolmen of Menga near Antequera in southern Spain is one of the largest stone tombs in Europe. Builders used 32 huge stone blocks, the biggest weighing about 180 tonnes, to make a long chamber, then covered it with earth to form a hill. When it was opened in the 19th century, it held the skeletons of several hundred people. Unusually, its entrance faces a nearby mountain, the Peña de los Enamorados, rather than the sunrise. It is part of the Antequera Dolmens World Heritage Site.

name: Maykop kurgan
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the tomb was dug in 1897 and is dated by comparing its objects and by radiocarbon dates from related graves.
summary: A burial mound about 10 m high in the town of Maykop in the North Caucasus of Russia, excavated by Nikolay Veselovsky in 1897. Under it lay a chieftain or 'priest-king' with rich grave goods, including gold and silver bull figurines, and the burials of two women. It gave its name to the Maykop culture, and its treasures are now in the Hermitage Museum. The mound itself no longer survives.

name: Ġgantija temples
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the temples are dated by pottery phases and radiocarbon.
summary: Ġgantija, on the island of Gozo, is the oldest of the Megalithic Temples of Malta. Its two temples, built around 3600 BCE from enormous limestone blocks, are older than Egypt's pyramids and among the oldest free-standing stone buildings in the world. Their name means 'place of giants', from a local legend that a giantess built them. Figurines found inside suggest religious rituals. Malta's temple-building culture ended around 2500 BCE.

image.caption: The Ġgantija temples on the Xagħra plateau, Gozo

name: Troy (Hisarlik)
evidenceNote: The city's ruins are real, and most scholars accept Hisarlik as Homer's Troy, but there is no firm proof that the Trojan War of legend happened.
summary: A mound near the Dardanelles in northwest Turkey with nine main layers of cities built on top of each other over about 4,000 years. Heinrich Schliemann and Frank Calvert dug it from 1871 looking for Homer's Troy. In the Late Bronze Age the city was probably the Wilusa named in Hittite texts, and one layer was destroyed around 1180 BCE. Whether any of this matches the war in the Iliad remains unproven.

image.caption: Walls of Bronze Age Troy

name: Watson Brake
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the mounds are dated by 27 radiocarbon dates published in Science in 1997.
summary: An oval ring of eleven earth mounds, up to about 7.5 metres high and joined by ridges, in the floodplain of the Ouachita River in Louisiana. Built in stages from about 3500 BCE for some 500 years, it is the oldest known mound complex in North America, older than Egypt's pyramids. Its builders were hunter-gatherers who fished and collected wild foods, which surprised archaeologists who had thought only farming societies could organise such work. The site is on private land and not open to visitors.

name: Sechín Bajo
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the oldest building, a sunken circular plaza, is dated by radiocarbon to about 3500 BCE.
summary: A large ceremonial site in the Sechín valley, a branch of the Casma valley on the north-central coast of Peru, about 12 km from the sea. In 2008 a German-Peruvian team announced a circular plaza 10–12 metres across dated to about 3500 BCE, which would make it one of the oldest monumental buildings in the Americas. Later platforms of stone and adobe were raised over sunken circular plazas for some 2,000 years. It stands among many early temples in the Casma valley, including nearby Cerro Sechín with its stone reliefs of warriors and sacrificed victims.

name: Laas Geel
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the paintings are dated by their style and by finds from the shelters, not by direct tests, so their age is an estimate.
summary: A group of rock shelters near Hargeisa in Somaliland, recorded by a French team of archaeologists in 2002. Their walls are covered with brightly painted long-horned cattle, some wearing decorative robes, with people standing beside them, as well as a dog, other canines and a giraffe. They are among the oldest and best-preserved paintings of herding in the Horn of Africa, estimated at about 5,500–4,500 years old.

name: Niuheliang
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the complex is dated by radiocarbon and by its Hongshan pottery and jades.
summary: Niuheliang, in western Liaoning, is a ritual and burial landscape of the late Hongshan culture, spread over hilltops covering about 50 square kilometres. Found in 1983, it includes the so-called Goddess Temple, where fragments of clay statues with jade eyes were found, along with stone altars and stone-lined cairn tombs. Elite graves held carved jades such as 'pig-dragons'. No houses have been found, which suggests it was a sacred centre visited from settlements elsewhere. It shows that complex religion and social ranks existed in northeast China around 3500–3000 BCE.

name: Ness of Brodgar
evidenceNote: No writing existed; excavations from 2003 to 2024 and radiocarbon dates tell its story.
summary: The Ness of Brodgar is a complex of large stone buildings on a strip of land between the Ring of Brodgar and the Stones of Stenness in Orkney, Scotland. Excavators found massive walls, decorated stone slabs and a large building described as a Neolithic temple. People gathered here for well over a thousand years, and by about 2200 BCE the site had been closed and partly taken apart. After excavation ended in 2024, it was covered over again to protect it.

name: Ebla (Tell Mardikh)
dateLabel: c. 3500 BCE – 7th century CE; archives c. 2400–2300 BCE
evidenceNote: Its own clay-tablet archive, written in cuneiform, names its kings and trade partners.
summary: A city southwest of Aleppo in Syria that became the strongest kingdom of the region in the 3rd millennium BCE. In its royal palace Paolo Matthiae's Italian team found an archive of thousands of clay tablets from about 2400–2300 BCE, written in a previously unknown language now called Eblaite. Its discovery proved that Syria had cities and states as old as those of Egypt and Mesopotamia.

image.caption: Excavated southern district of Ebla

name: Sarazm
evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavations since 1977 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A proto-urban settlement on the Zeravshan river near Panjakent, Tajikistan, and Tajikistan's first World Heritage Site. At its height it covered up to 90 hectares, with houses and workshops where copper and bronze were worked with techniques like those of Mesopotamia, Iran and the Indus. Pottery from Turkmenistan and Baluchistan shows its wide contacts, and it may have been a centre for mining turquoise and metals in the Zeravshan valley. It shows farming towns reaching the northern edge of Central Asia long before the steppe herders came.

image.caption: Excavation area XII under a protective roof

name: Kalibangan
evidenceNote: The Indus script cannot be read; the site is known from excavations of 1960–1969 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Harappan town on the dry Ghaggar river in Rajasthan with two phases. The earlier, walled settlement (about 3500–2600 BCE) left the world's earliest excavated ploughed field, marked with criss-cross furrows, and was ended by an earthquake around 2600 BCE. The rebuilt mature town had a fortified citadel on the west, a lower town of grid streets, and rows of fire altars that suggest ritual. Seals, weights and pottery tie it to Harappa and Mohenjo-daro.

image.caption: The western mound (citadel)

name: Liangzhu City
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the city, its walls and dams were dated by radiocarbon during excavations since the 1930s and especially after 2007.
summary: Liangzhu, near Hangzhou in Zhejiang, was the centre of the Liangzhu culture of the lower Yangtze. In 2007 archaeologists announced a walled city enclosing about 290 hectares, with six gates and an elite platform, and later found a system of dams and dykes upstream for water control. Elite graves were full of finely carved jade, especially cong tubes and bi discs. Liangzhu is often described as one of the earliest early states in East Asia, built on rice farming. UNESCO listed the archaeological ruins of Liangzhu City in 2019.

name: Harappa
dateLabel: c. 3300–1300 BCE; city at its height c. 2600–1900 BCE
evidenceNote: Thousands of short inscriptions survive, but the Indus script is undeciphered, so the city is known from excavation and radiocarbon dates.
summary: The first Indus city to be excavated, in the 1920s, which gave the Harappan civilisation its name. Near the old course of the Ravi in Pakistani Punjab, it grew from a village around 3300 BCE into a walled city of perhaps 23,500 people, with brick houses, drains, granary-like halls, workshops and cemeteries. Seals, standard weights and beads show long-distance trade. Much of its brick was taken for railway ballast in 1857. Late layers include the 'Cemetery H' burials.

image.caption: Granary and Great Hall on Mound F

name: Kot Diji
evidenceNote: No readable writing; known from excavations in 1955–57 and comparison with other dated sites.
summary: A fortified settlement in Sindh, Pakistan, across the Indus from Mohenjo-daro, which gave its name to the Kot Diji phase of the Early Harappan period. Excavations in 1955 and 1957 found a walled citadel on high ground and a town around it, with mudbrick houses and pottery of a style that spread across the region. Its later layers run on into the Mature Harappan period, showing how the regional cultures of the Indus valley grew into one civilisation. The hill above it is crowned by an 18th-century fort.

name: Ötzi the Iceman (find site)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; his body and equipment have been studied scientifically since 1991.
summary: In 1991 two hikers found a man's body coming out of the ice near the Tisenjoch pass, 3,210 metres up in the Alps on the Austria–Italy border. Ötzi lived more than 5,300 years ago and is Europe's oldest known natural mummy. He carried a copper axe, a flint knife, a longbow and a quiver of arrows, and wore leather clothes and a bearskin cap. An arrowhead in his shoulder shows that he was killed by another person. His body is now kept at the South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology in Bolzano.

sources.title: South Tyrol Museum of Archaeology: Ötzi the Iceman

name: Altyn-Depe
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dated by Soviet and later excavations since 1965 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A Bronze Age town on the edge of the Kopet Dag near the Iran border in Turkmenistan. By the late third millennium BCE it covered about 25 hectares inside a mudbrick wall, with craftsmen's quarters, rich houses and a stepped, tower-like temple platform often compared to a ziggurat. Finds include Harappan-style seals and ivory, evidence of contact with the Indus cities. It was abandoned around 2000 BCE as settlement shifted east to the Murghab delta and the BMAC towns.

image.caption: The mound of the ancient town

name: Skara Brae
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates and excavation tell us when people lived here.
summary: Skara Brae, on the west coast of Orkney's Mainland, is Europe's most complete Neolithic village. A storm in 1850 uncovered stone houses buried in sand dunes. Each house was a single room joined to the others by covered passages and had built-in stone furniture: a 'dresser', box beds and a central hearth. Farmers lived here from about 3180 to 2500 BCE. No one knows why the village was abandoned: some think sand buried it, others that people left gradually. It is part of the Heart of Neolithic Orkney World Heritage Site.

image.caption: A house with stone furniture at Skara Brae

sources.title: Historic Environment Scotland: Skara Brae, history

name: Newgrange
dateLabel: built c. 3100 BCE; out of use by the Bronze Age
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from the building and excavations from 1962 to 1975 tell us its age.
summary: Newgrange in County Meath, Ireland, is a huge passage tomb built around 3100 BCE, older than Stonehenge and the pyramids of Giza. A stone passage leads into a cross-shaped chamber inside a round mound ringed by carved kerbstones. At sunrise on the winter solstice, light shines through a 'roof-box' over the entrance and fills the chamber. Burnt and unburnt human bones were found inside. By the start of the Bronze Age it was falling into ruin. It is the main monument of the Brú na Bóinne World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The restored white quartz front of Newgrange

name: Stonehenge
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dating of antler picks, bones and pits shows its building phases, but its purpose is still debated.
summary: Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in England was built in stages from about 3100 to 1600 BCE. It began as a circular ditch and bank. The great ring of sarsen stones, each about 25 tonnes and topped by lintels joined with woodworking-style joints, was put up between about 2600 and 2400 BCE. Smaller bluestones were brought from Wales. The monument lines up with sunrise at the summer solstice and sunset at the winter solstice, and hundreds of burial mounds surround it.

image.caption: Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain

name: Lothagam North Pillar Site
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the cemetery is dated by radiocarbon, published in 2018; the location shown is approximate.
summary: A monumental cemetery on the west side of Lake Turkana in northern Kenya, built by eastern Africa's earliest herders about 5,000 years ago. A platform about 700 m² was dug down to bedrock and filled with at least 580 burials of men, women and children of all ages, nearly all with beads and ornaments, then capped and ringed with boulders. Natural basalt pillars were set up on top. It shows that early herders built large monuments together while the lake shrank and climate changed.

image.caption: Basalt pillars and stones at the Lothagam North Pillar Site

sources.title: Hildebrand et al. 2018, PNAS: A monumental cemetery built by eastern Africa's first herders near Lake Turkana, Kenya

name: Los Millares
evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates and excavations since the 1890s tell its story.
summary: Los Millares, near Almería in southern Spain, was a fortified Copper Age town of perhaps 1,000 people. Three rings of stone walls with bastions protected it, and four small forts guarded the approach. Inside were simple houses and a workshop for smelting copper. Outside lay a cemetery of about 80 passage-grave tombs. It was found in 1891 during railway building and first dug by Luis Siret. It is the type site of the Los Millares culture.

name: Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn
evidenceNote: No local writing survives; the tombs and towers are dated by excavation, while Sumerian texts mention a copper land called Magan.
summary: A group of Bronze Age sites in inland Oman. Hundreds of stone 'beehive' tombs line the ridges, and round stone towers stood near a palm grove. They belong to the Hafit and Umm an-Nar periods, when this region exported copper and stone to Mesopotamia; the area is usually identified with the land of Magan in Sumerian texts. Together they form one of the most complete Bronze Age landscapes in Arabia, a UNESCO site since 1988.

image.caption: A beehive tomb at Al-Ayn, part of the Bat World Heritage group

sources.title: Wikipedia: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn

name: Nineveh
dateLabel: c. 3000–612 BCE (Assyrian capital from c. 700 BCE)
evidenceNote: Named in Assyrian royal inscriptions and the Bible; its palace libraries held tens of thousands of tablets.
summary: An ancient city on the east bank of the Tigris opposite Mosul in northern Iraq. Under Sennacherib it became the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire and for a few decades probably the largest city in the world, with huge palaces, gates and canals. The library of Ashurbanipal, dug up here, held about 22,000 clay tablets. Nineveh was sacked in 612 BCE by Babylonians, Medes and others. Parts of the site were damaged during the war with ISIS.

image.caption: The reconstructed Mashki Gate of Nineveh, later destroyed by the Islamic State

name: Dholavira
evidenceNote: The Indus script is undeciphered; dates come from excavations of 1990–2005 and radiocarbon, and scholars still argue over its phases.
summary: A Harappan city on Khadir Bet island in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat, and a World Heritage Site since 2021. Built of stone as well as brick, it had a castle, a 'middle town' and a lower town, all walled, and a remarkable system of dams, channels and great rock-cut reservoirs to store scarce rain. A signboard of ten large Indus signs, once set in wood, was found by the north gate. Its dates are debated, from about 3500–1800 to 2650–1450 BCE.

image.caption: Stone walls and the reservoir steps

name: Burzahom
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dated by radiocarbon, which puts the first occupation before about 2350 BCE.
summary: A Neolithic village near Srinagar in the Kashmir Valley. Its first farmers lived in pit dwellings dug into the ground, some with steps, and made bone and polished stone tools, including harvesting knives like those of China. Bones of dogs and deer were found buried with people, and a carved stone shows a hunting scene. Later people built mudbrick houses and raised large standing stones (menhirs). The finds show contacts with Central Asia and the Indus world.

name: Step Pyramid of Djoser, Saqqara
evidenceNote: Built for a king whose name is written in the complex, and dated by Egyptian king lists and radiocarbon.
summary: The first Egyptian pyramid, built in the 27th century BCE at Saqqara near Memphis for King Djoser of the Third Dynasty. Its six stacked steps grew out of several changes of plan, and it was once covered in white limestone. It is the earliest colossal building in Egypt made of cut stone, and the start of the pyramid age. Later Egyptians credited its design to the official Imhotep.

image.caption: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara

name: Caral (Sacred City of Caral-Supe)
evidenceNote: No writing existed (a knotted string found here may be an early quipu record); the city is dated by radiocarbon since Ruth Shady's excavations.
summary: The best-known city of the Caral-Supe (Norte Chico) civilization, set on a dry terrace above the Supe valley, 23 km from the Peruvian coast. It has large platform mounds, sunken circular plazas and homes for elites and workers; finds include cotton textiles and 32 flutes of condor and pelican bone, but no pottery. Built while the Egyptian pyramids were rising, it is considered the oldest city in the Americas. Fishing towns such as nearby Áspero traded seafood for cotton and crops. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Great Pyramid and a sunken circular plaza at Caral

name: Pyramids of Giza
evidenceNote: The pyramids are dated by Egyptian king lists, workers' graffiti naming the kings, and radiocarbon.
summary: The burial complex of three kings of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty, Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, at the edge of the desert west of Cairo. Khufu's Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for almost 4,000 years and is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing. The site also includes the Great Sphinx, temples, cemeteries for officials, and the village of the workers who built them.

image.caption: The pyramids of Giza

name: Kerma
evidenceNote: The Kerma people left no writing of their own; we know them from excavation and from Egyptian records that call their land Kush.
summary: Capital of the first great kingdom of Nubia, beside the Nile in northern Sudan. Its centre was the Western Deffufa, a massive mudbrick temple that still towers over the ruins. In the great cemetery to the east, rulers were buried under round mounds with cattle skulls and, in later periods, sacrificed people. At its peak, about 1750–1500 BCE, Kerma was a rival of Egypt, until the armies of Thutmose I campaigned south and destroyed it.

image.caption: The Western Deffufa, the great mudbrick temple of Kerma

name: Mohenjo-daro
evidenceNote: The Indus script cannot be read and the city's real name is unknown; it is known from excavations since the 1920s.
summary: The largest and best-preserved Indus city, beside the Indus in Sindh, Pakistan, and South Asia's first World Heritage Site (1980). At least 40,000 people may have lived in its baked-brick houses, laid out on a grid with covered drains, wells and bathrooms. A raised 'citadel' mound holds the Great Bath and a large hall. Famous finds include the bronze 'Dancing Girl', the 'Priest-King' statue and many stamp seals. It declined after about 1900 BCE and was abandoned.

image.caption: The citadel mound, with a later Buddhist stupa on top

name: Gonur Depe
evidenceNote: No writing has been found; dated by radiocarbon and by excavations from 1974 to 2013.
summary: The largest centre of the Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, in the old Murghab delta north of Merv, Turkmenistan. Excavated by Viktor Sarianidi, its fortified core held a palace, courtyards and buildings he saw as fire temples, inside walls with rectangular towers. A cemetery of more than 3,000 graves included rich tombs, one with a four-wheeled wagon and a foal, and goods linked to Iran and the Indus. Sarianidi's 'temple' readings are much debated.

name: Mausoleum of Tangun
dateLabel: legendary date 2333 BCE; present monument built 1994
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found that Tangun was a real person or that bones in this tomb belong to him.
summary: Korean tradition, first written down in the 13th-century Samguk yusa, says that Tangun, son of a heavenly prince and a bear-woman, founded the first Korean kingdom, Gojoseon, in 2333 BCE. In 1993 North Korea announced that bones found in a tomb near Pyongyang were Tangun's and about 5,000 years old, and built a large stone pyramid there in 1994. Scholars outside North Korea do not accept the claim: a nail of Goguryeo date (37 BCE–668 CE) found in the tomb is part of the controversy, and Gojoseon itself appears in Chinese records only many centuries after 2333 BCE.

name: Shimao
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the walls and buildings are dated by radiocarbon and by finds from recent excavations.
summary: Shimao, in Shenmu County on the northern Loess Plateau of Shaanxi, is the largest known walled site of its time in China, covering about 400 hectares. Its stone walls were once mistaken for part of the Great Wall. At its heart stood a stepped pyramid built from a reshaped loess hill with 11 platforms, about 70 metres high, decorated with carved stone faces and figures. Jade pieces were set into the walls, and there is evidence of human sacrifice. Shimao shows that powerful centres existed outside the Central Plains. A cooler, drier climate after about 2000 BCE probably led to its abandonment.

name: Taosi
evidenceNote: No writing has been read from Taosi; it is dated by radiocarbon, and claims that it was the capital of the legendary Emperor Yao are unproven.
summary: Taosi, in Xiangfen County in southern Shanxi, was the largest Longshan-period centre in the Linfen basin. In its middle phase a rammed-earth wall enclosed about 280 hectares, and an inner wall separated an elite quarter from commoners, showing a strongly ranked society. A semicircular platform with pillars has been interpreted as an early astronomical observatory used to track sunrise for a calendar. Rich graves held painted pottery, drums and jade. Some Chinese scholars link Taosi with the legendary sage-king Yao, but no written evidence confirms this.

name: Babylon
dateLabel: c. 2300 BCE – c. 1000 CE; first mentioned c. 2200 BCE
evidenceNote: Babylon appears in thousands of cuneiform texts, in Greek histories and in the Bible.
summary: The great city on the Euphrates south of Baghdad, capital of Hammurabi's kingdom in the 18th century BCE and of Nebuchadnezzar II's empire in the 6th century BCE. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt it with massive walls, the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate and the temple of Marduk with its ziggurat, Etemenanki. The Hanging Gardens may never have existed: no Babylonian text mentions them. Babylon became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

image.caption: Modern replica of the Ishtar Gate at Babylon (the original bricks are in Berlin)

name: Lothal
evidenceNote: The Indus script is undeciphered; dated by the 1955–60 excavations and radiocarbon, and the use of its big basin is disputed.
summary: One of the southernmost Indus towns, in Gujarat near the Gulf of Khambhat. Excavated from 1955, it had a raised acropolis, a lower town with drains, and bead-making workshops of carnelian and shell. Its most famous feature is a large brick basin that the excavator S. R. Rao identified as the world's oldest dock, linked to a river channel; other archaeologists think it was a water tank for irrigation or storage. Floods damaged the town around 1900 BCE.

image.caption: Brick drains and bathing platforms

name: El Argar
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dates come from graves and layers excavated since the 1880s.
summary: El Argar, on a flat hilltop near Antas in Almería, southeastern Spain, is the type site of the Early Bronze Age Argaric culture. Behind a wall stood rows of long rectangular houses, and more than a thousand graves were dug inside the houses themselves, many with bronze daggers, axes and ornaments. The Argaric people were among the first in Iberia to use bronze widely, and some archaeologists think their society was ruled like an early state.

name: Dilmun Burial Mounds
evidenceNote: The mounds are dated by excavation; Mesopotamian texts describe Dilmun as a trading land in the Gulf.
summary: Thousands of burial mounds across the north of Bahrain, once one of the largest ancient cemeteries in the world; an estimated 350,000 graves may have existed. Most were built during the time of Dilmun, the Gulf trading civilisation that linked Mesopotamia with the Indus Valley; Bahrain's freshwater springs made it a natural stop for ships. The surviving mound fields became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019.

image.caption: Burial mounds in Bahrain, photographed in 1918

name: Arkaim
evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from excavations since 1987 and radiocarbon dates.
summary: A circular fortified settlement of the Sintashta culture in the southern Urals, discovered in 1987 just before the valley was to be flooded for a reservoir; the find saved it. Two rings of walls enclosed about sixty houses arranged like the spokes of a wheel, each with a hearth, well and copper furnace. It is now a protected reserve. The find also set off far-fetched nationalist speculation, which archaeologists reject.

image.caption: Aerial view of the ring-shaped settlement

name: Sintashta
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dated by radiocarbon from excavations since 1968.
summary: A fortified settlement in the steppe east of the southern Urals, in Russia, and the type site of the Sintashta culture. Ditches and walls ringed some fifty or sixty houses, of which thirty-one survive the river's erosion, and so much copper-working was found that it is called a fortified metallurgical centre. Its graves hold some of the earliest known chariots, with spoked wheels, buried with horses and weapons. Many scholars link Sintashta to early speakers of Indo-Iranian languages.

name: Dhar Tichitt
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the villages are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal and millet impressions in pottery.
summary: A line of sandstone cliffs in southeastern Mauritania with hundreds of stone-walled villages built by herders and farmers when the area was savanna. The settlements have drystone compounds with houses and granaries, linked by streets, and some, such as Dakhlet el Atrouss, were very large. Its people kept cattle, sheep and goats, hunted, fished, and grew bulrush (pearl) millet. Dhar Tichitt is one of the oldest known village societies in West Africa and may have been a regional centre.

name: Ban Chiang
dateLabel: c. 2000 or 1500 BCE – c. 200 CE (start date disputed)
evidenceNote: No writing existed, and archaeologists disagree about when the village began and when bronze appeared, by as much as 1,000 years.
summary: Ban Chiang, in Udon Thani Province, northeast Thailand, became famous after 1966 for its red-painted pottery and its long sequence of burials. Early tests suggested bronze-working here as early as the fourth millennium BCE, which would have been the oldest in the world, but later dating rejected this. Today one team argues that settlement began around 2000 BCE with bronze soon after, while another, using Bayesian analysis of dates on human bone, puts first settlement around 1500 BCE and bronze around 1000 BCE. The last graves date to about 200 CE. UNESCO listed Ban Chiang in 1992.

name: Ōyu Stone Circles
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the circles are dated by the late Jōmon pottery found with them.
summary: The Ōyu Stone Circles, in Kazuno, Akita Prefecture, are two large rings of river stones built on a levelled plateau during the late Jōmon period. The larger, Manza circle is 46 metres across, the largest stone circle in Japan. Each ring is made of many small stone settings, some with an upright stone like a sundial, and pits beneath may be graves. There is no sign of permanent houses on the site, so it was probably a place for ceremonies and burial. It is part of the UNESCO-listed Jōmon sites of northern Japan.

image.caption: Stone settings at the Ōyu Stone Circles, Akita

name: Hattusa
dateLabel: c. 2000–1190 BCE (Hittite capital from c. 1650 BCE)
evidenceNote: Tens of thousands of clay tablets found in the city record Hittite laws, treaties and letters.
summary: The capital of the Hittite kings, inside a bend of the Kızılırmak River in central Turkey. Its walls, gates guarded by stone lions and sphinxes, temples and palaces covered a hilly site of about 1.8 km². Its archives of clay tablets, and a bronze tablet recording a treaty between King Tudhaliya IV and Kurunta of Tarhuntassa, reveal Hittite politics. The city was abandoned around 1190 BCE when the Hittite empire collapsed.

image.caption: The Lion Gate in the walls of Hattusa

name: Palmyra
dateLabel: early 2nd millennium BCE – 1932 CE; height 1st–3rd century CE
evidenceNote: Palmyra is named in texts from about 2000 BCE, and thousands of its own inscriptions survive.
summary: An oasis city in the Syrian desert that grew rich on caravan trade between the Roman Empire, Mesopotamia and beyond. Its merchants paid for the Great Colonnade, the Temple of Bel (dedicated in 32 CE) and tall tower tombs. In the 260s its rulers Odaenathus and then Queen Zenobia briefly controlled much of the Roman East, until Rome sacked the city in 273 CE. ISIS blew up the Temple of Bel and other monuments in 2015.

image.caption: Ruins of Palmyra with the Temple of Bel behind (photo before 2015)

name: Shortugai
evidenceNote: Known from French excavations in the 1970s; its Harappan seals and pottery date it alongside the Indus cities.
summary: The northernmost Indus settlement, on the Amu Darya (Oxus) in northern Afghanistan, more than 1,000 km from the Indus. French archaeologists found Harappan pottery, a seal with a rhinoceros, beads and bricks of Indus proportions. It was most likely a trading post near the lapis lazuli mines of Badakhshan, collecting the deep-blue stone and perhaps tin for the Indus cities. Irrigation canals fed its fields. Later layers show influence from the local Bronze Age cultures.

name: Sinauli
evidenceNote: The burials and carts are real and dated to around 2000–1500 BCE, but whether the carts were horse-drawn war chariots, and who the people were, is argued over.
summary: A Bronze Age cemetery in western Uttar Pradesh, excavated in 2005–06 and 2018. It held many burials, some in wooden coffins decorated with copper, with copper swords, shields, a helmet and pottery. In 2018 three carts with solid wooden wheels covered in copper sheet were found in graves. The excavators called them chariots and linked them to warriors of the Vedic or Harappan world; other archaeologists say solid wheels suit ox-carts and place the site in the Ochre Coloured Pottery culture.

name: Karnak Temple Complex
evidenceNote: Its walls are covered with hieroglyphic inscriptions naming the kings who built each part.
summary: The vast temple of the god Amun at Thebes (modern Luxor), the main religious centre of New Kingdom Egypt. Building began under Senusret I around 1970 BCE and continued for nearly 2,000 years, into Ptolemaic times. Its Great Hypostyle Hall has 134 giant columns. A processional avenue lined with sphinxes connected it to Luxor Temple. Karnak is part of the UNESCO site of Ancient Thebes.

image.caption: Hall of columns at Karnak, in a 19th-century photograph

name: Knossos (Palace of Minos)
dateLabel: palace c. 1900–1350 BCE (hill settled from c. 7000 BCE)
evidenceNote: Late clay tablets in Linear B (early Greek) name Knossos as Ko-no-so, but the Minoans' own Linear A script is undeciphered, so most of its history comes from excavation.
summary: Knossos, just south of Heraklion on Crete, was the largest centre of the Minoan civilisation. People settled the hill around 7000 BCE. The first palace, built around 1900 BCE, was rebuilt after a destruction around 1700 BCE into a huge complex of courtyards, storerooms, shrines and painted halls. It was probably a centre of government, trade and religion. Thousands of Linear B tablets were found there. Arthur Evans dug it from 1900 and rebuilt parts in concrete, which still shapes how visitors see it.

name: Paso de la Amada
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site is dated by radiocarbon and by its pottery, which belongs to the Mokaya tradition.
summary: A village of the Mokaya people on the Pacific coastal plain of Chiapas, Mexico, covering about 50 hectares. It holds the oldest known Mesoamerican ballcourt, a long earthen court built around 1650 BCE, centuries before the Olmec heyday, showing that the famous ball game is very old. Large house platforms that grew over time suggest that some families were gaining rank, an early sign of social inequality in the region. Later pottery shows contact with the Olmecs.

name: Etemenanki, the ziggurat of Babylon
dateLabel: origins perhaps 18th century BCE; rebuilt 7th–6th century BCE; demolished 323 BCE
evidenceNote: The ziggurat is described in Babylonian inscriptions and a tablet giving its size; only its foundation outline survives.
summary: The great stepped temple tower of the god Marduk in Babylon, whose name means 'Temple of the Foundation of Heaven and Earth'. Damaged when Sennacherib sacked Babylon in 689 BCE, it was rebuilt by Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II. A later tablet claims it was 91 m high and wide, a figure modern scholars doubt. Alexander the Great had it pulled down in 323 BCE to rebuild it, but died first. Today only a water-filled square marks its base.

name: Erlitou
dateLabel: c. 1750–1500 BCE (older estimates from c. 1900 BCE)
evidenceNote: The city is real and dated by radiocarbon, but no writing has been found there, so whether it was a capital of the Xia dynasty is debated.
summary: Erlitou, near Yanshi in Henan, is the type site of the Erlitou culture and is seen by most archaeologists as the centre of China's first state-level society. It had large palace compounds on rammed-earth platforms, roads, a walled palace area and workshops, and it monopolised the casting of ritual bronze vessels, including the earliest known ding. Many Chinese archaeologists identify it with the later Xia dynasty of traditional histories, but because no contemporary writing has been found, many Western scholars consider that identification unproven. After about 1600 BCE nearby Yanshi took over.

name: Poverty Point
