evidenceNote: No writing existed; the earthworks are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal from mound layers.
summary: A vast set of earthworks on Macon Ridge in northeastern Louisiana: six concentric C-shaped ridges about 1.2 km across, facing a bayou, plus several large mounds, the first being Mound B soon after 1700 BCE. It was built by hunter-fisher-gatherers, not farmers, who imported soapstone vessels from the Appalachian foothills. It may have been a place where groups met to trade and hold ceremonies. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed in 2014.

image.caption: Mound B at Poverty Point

name: Sanxingdui
evidenceNote: No readable writing has been found at Sanxingdui; it is dated by radiocarbon, and its link to the later kingdom of Shu comes from much later texts.
summary: Sanxingdui, in Guanghan near Chengdu in Sichuan, was a walled city of a Bronze Age culture quite different from the Shang to the north. In 1986 archaeologists found two pits filled with deliberately broken and burned treasures: bronze heads and masks with bulging eyes, some covered in gold foil, an upright bronze figure, gold, jade and pottery, radiocarbon dated to the 12th–11th centuries BCE. New pits excavated from 2021 produced hundreds more objects, including a gold mask. Many archaeologists link the culture to the ancient kingdom of Shu, but the people left no writing that has been read.

name: Su Nuraxi di Barumini
dateLabel: tower 17th–13th century BCE; village to the 6th century BCE
evidenceNote: The Nuragic people left no writing; dates come from excavations begun in the 1950s and radiocarbon.
summary: Su Nuraxi ('the nuraghe') at Barumini is the finest example of Sardinia's nuraghi: stone towers built by the Nuragic civilisation. Its central basalt tower, with three chambers stacked inside, rose about 18.6 metres. Later four corner towers and a curtain wall were added around it, and a village of round stone huts grew outside from the 13th to the 6th century BCE. Archaeologists still debate whether nuraghi were mainly fortresses, homes of leaders or religious buildings. Giovanni Lilliu excavated it in the 1950s.

image.caption: The nuraghe of Su Nuraxi at Barumini

name: Zhengzhou Shang City
evidenceNote: The city is dated by radiocarbon and pottery phases; very little writing has been found there, so which Shang capital it was is uncertain.
summary: Under modern Zhengzhou in Henan lie the remains of a great city of the Erligang culture, the early phase of the Shang dynasty. Found in 1950, it was enclosed by massive rammed-earth walls, parts of which still stand in the modern city, and archaeologists have dug outside them since 1952. Large bronze ding cauldrons from the site show the wealth of its rulers. It was probably one of the early Shang capitals, but scholars disagree whether it was the capital called Bo or Ao in later texts. It was occupied in four phases from about 1600 to 1400 BCE.

name: Mycenae
dateLabel: citadel c. 1600–1100 BCE (Lion Gate c. 1250 BCE)
evidenceNote: Linear B clay tablets in early Greek were found here, and later Greek writers describe it; Homer's King Agamemnon, though, belongs to legend.
summary: Mycenae, on a hill in the Argolid, gave its name to the Mycenaean civilisation of Bronze Age Greece. Rich shaft graves full of gold date from around 1600 BCE. Around 1250 BCE its walls of giant 'Cyclopean' blocks were extended and the Lion Gate built, crowned by two carved lions or lionesses. The Treasury of Atreus is a vast beehive-shaped tomb. Mycenae was destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse around 1200 BCE and survived only as a small town until 468 BCE.

image.caption: The path up to the Lion Gate, Mycenae

name: Nebra sky disc find site (Mittelberg)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the disc was dug up illegally in 1999, so its date rests on scientific tests and the objects buried with it; most experts accept a Bronze Age date, though a 2020 paper argued for a later one.
summary: In 1999 treasure hunters with a metal detector illegally dug up a bronze disc on the Mittelberg hill near Nebra, Germany. The state archaeologist recovered it in a police sting in 2002. The disc, inlaid with gold, shows the Sun or full Moon, a crescent Moon and stars, including a cluster thought to be the Pleiades. It is the oldest known concrete picture of the sky, buried around 1600 BCE by people of the Únětice culture. It is now in the State Museum of Prehistory in Halle and on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

sources.title: State Museum of Prehistory Halle: Nebra Sky Disc

name: San José Mogote
evidenceNote: Mostly archaeology dated by radiocarbon; one carved stone of about 600 BCE may carry the earliest Zapotec writing, but it can barely be read.
summary: The largest village in the Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico, from about 1500 to 500 BCE and the forerunner of Monte Albán. It is thought to be the oldest permanent farming village in the valley and has some of Mexico's oldest ceremonial buildings and defensive palisades, from about 1300 BCE. A carved stone (Monument 3) of about 600 BCE showing a slain man, with two glyphs that may give his name, '1 Earthquake', may be the earliest Zapotec writing. Its people seem to have moved to the new hilltop city of Monte Albán.

image.caption: The main stairs of the pyramid at San José Mogote

name: Kaminaljuyu
evidenceNote: Known mainly from excavation and radiocarbon dates; much of the site was destroyed by building before it could be studied.
summary: A large Maya city in the highland Valley of Guatemala, now mostly buried under Guatemala City. When first mapped it had about 200 platforms and pyramid mounds built of hardened adobe. Its peak came in the Miraflores period, about 400–100 BCE, when rulers were buried in rich tombs inside a series of mounds, and the southern Maya area it led is thought to have shaped later Maya culture. Only a small part survives as a city park of about 0.5 km².

image.caption: Excavated part of the Acropolis at Kaminaljuyu, under a protective roof

name: Nok
dateLabel: c. 1500 BCE – 1 CE; terracottas from c. 900 BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon and luminescence on excavated sites; the point marks the area of Nok village.
summary: The village in southern Kaduna State, Nigeria, where Nok terracotta sculptures were first found in 1928, giving its name to the whole culture. Nok sculptures are hollow fired-clay figures and heads with large triangular or D-shaped eyes, carefully styled hair and jewellery, made from about 900 BCE. Some show people with slings or bows and arrows. They are among the oldest figurative sculptures south of the Sahara, and may have been part of funeral customs.

image.caption: Nok terracotta figure, now in the Louvre

name: Submerged structures off Dwarka
dateLabel: disputed: c. 1500 BCE (S. R. Rao) or historical to medieval times
evidenceNote: Real stone walls and anchors lie on the sea floor, but their age is disputed and nothing proves they are Krishna's city of the epics.
summary: Divers of India's National Institute of Oceanography explored the sea off Dwarka and Bet Dwarka in Gujarat from 1983. They found stone blocks, walls and many stone anchors. The excavator S. R. Rao argued that they belonged to a city of about 1500 BCE and identified it with Dvaraka, Krishna's capital in the Mahabharata, which the epic says was swallowed by the sea. Later surveys compared the anchors to types used from ancient to late medieval times and dated the structures to the historical period. Dwarka is a sacred pilgrimage town.

name: San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán
evidenceNote: No readable writing survives; the site is dated by radiocarbon and by its pottery sequence.
summary: The first great centre of the Olmec civilization, on a raised plateau above the river plains of southern Veracruz, Mexico. From about 1400 to 900 BCE its rulers commissioned colossal basalt heads up to about 3.4 metres tall and weighing as much as 28 tonnes, along with huge stone thrones. Builders moved hundreds of thousands of cubic metres of earth to level the plateau and laid lines of U-shaped stone drains, showing organised work on a big scale. Leadership later shifted to La Venta.

name: Luxor Temple
evidenceNote: Inscriptions on the temple name its builders, Amenhotep III, Tutankhamun, Ramesses II and Alexander.
summary: A large temple on the east bank of the Nile in Luxor (ancient Thebes), begun around 1400 BCE by Amenhotep III. It was dedicated to the renewal of kingship, and statues of Amun were carried here from Karnak each year in the Opet festival. Ramesses II added the front pylon, colossal statues and two obelisks; one now stands in Paris. In Roman times it became part of a legionary fort, and a mosque still stands on its walls.

image.caption: Entrance pylon and obelisk of Luxor Temple at night

name: Abu Simbel temples
evidenceNote: Inscriptions carved in the temples name Ramesses II and his queen Nefertari.
summary: Two temples cut into a sandstone cliff in Nubia, in the far south of Egypt, by Ramesses II in the 13th century BCE. Four colossal seated statues of the king guard the Great Temple, while the smaller temple honours Queen Nefertari; reliefs inside celebrate his battle of Kadesh. In the 1960s an international campaign cut both temples into blocks and moved them uphill, away from the rising waters of Lake Nasser.

image.caption: The Great and Small Temples at Abu Simbel

name: Yinxu (Anyang)
evidenceNote: Thousands of inscribed oracle bones found here name Shang kings, so this site is known from its own writing as well as from excavation.
summary: Yinxu, at Anyang in Henan, was the last capital of the Shang dynasty during the Late Shang period, about 1250–1046 BCE, spanning the reigns of 12 kings. Excavations since 1928 have revealed palace and temple foundations, royal tombs, chariot burials and bronze workshops. Most importantly, the site produced tens of thousands of oracle bones: turtle shells and ox bones inscribed with questions to the ancestors. They are the earliest known Chinese writing. The tomb of Fu Hao, a queen and military leader, was found intact in 1976. UNESCO listed Yinxu in 2006.

name: Chogha Zanbil
evidenceNote: Inscribed bricks name its gods, and Elamite records link it to King Untash-Napirisha.
summary: A religious city of the Elamite king Untash-Napirisha in Khuzestan, southwestern Iran, southeast of Susa. Its centre is one of the few ziggurats outside Mesopotamia and the best preserved anywhere; thousands of its bricks carry inscriptions. The city is usually thought to have been destroyed by the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal around 645 BCE, though some researchers think it was abandoned much earlier. It was Iran's first UNESCO site, in 1979.

image.caption: The Elamite ziggurat of Chogha Zanbil

name: Plain of Jars
dateLabel: jars placed perhaps c. 1240–660 BCE; burials at Site 1 8th–13th centuries CE
evidenceNote: The jars are real, but dating them is hard: one study puts them in place over 2,500 years ago, while burials around them are much later.
summary: The Plain of Jars, on the Xiangkhoang Plateau of Laos, is a landscape of thousands of carved stone jars, some weighing several tonnes, grouped at more than 100 sites. Madeleine Colani's 1930s excavations linked them to burial, finding bones, beads and pottery. Recent work showed the stone at Site 1 was hauled from a quarry 8 km away. Optically stimulated luminescence suggests some jars were placed between about 1240 and 660 BCE, but excavations at Site 1 found secondary burials from the 8th to 13th centuries CE, so how long the jars were used is still debated. UNESCO listed it in 2019.

image.caption: Stone jars at Site 1, Plain of Jars, Laos

name: Chavín de Huántar
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the temple is dated by radiocarbon, though experts still argue over exactly when its main phases began and ended.
summary: A temple complex at 3,180 metres in the Andes of north-central Peru, where two rivers meet. Its stone platforms hide narrow galleries; at the very centre stands the Lanzón, a tall carved stone thought to show the temple's supreme god. Reliefs show jaguars, caimans and other creatures with human features. Placed between the coast and the Amazon, it drew pilgrims and traders, and its art style spread across much of Peru. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The temple platforms of Chavín de Huántar in their Andean valley

name: La Venta
evidenceNote: No readable writing survives; the site is dated by radiocarbon and by comparing its carvings and pottery with other Olmec sites.
summary: An Olmec capital on an island in the coastal swamps of Tabasco, Mexico, which became the main Olmec centre after San Lorenzo declined. Its clay Great Pyramid is one of the oldest pyramids in Mesoamerica. Builders buried mosaic pavements of nearly 500 serpentine blocks, 'massive offerings' of serpentine and more than 50 caches of jade and polished mirrors, and set up colossal heads, thrones and carved stelae. Many of its monuments now stand in the Parque-Museo La Venta in Villahermosa. The centre was abandoned around 400 BCE.

image.caption: North face of the clay Great Pyramid at La Venta

name: Jinsha
evidenceNote: No writing has been found; the site is dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles since its discovery in 2001.
summary: Jinsha, in the western suburbs of Chengdu, Sichuan, was discovered by chance in February 2001 during building work. It became the main centre of the Chengdu Plain after the decline of Sanxingdui, and is often described as a capital of the ancient Shu. Excavations found thousands of gold, bronze, jade, stone and ivory objects, many in ritual deposits. Its best-known find, a thin gold disc with four birds circling a sun, was chosen as a symbol of Chinese cultural heritage. A museum now stands over the excavation.

image.caption: Excavation hall at the Jinsha Site Museum, Chengdu

name: Hallstatt salt mines and cemetery
evidenceNote: No writing existed here; the story comes from more than a thousand excavated graves and finds in the salt mines.
summary: High above the lake town of Hallstatt in Austria, people mined rock salt from the Bronze Age onward. Salt was precious for preserving food, and the trade made the community rich. From 1846 Johann Georg Ramsauer excavated a huge prehistoric cemetery here, with more than a thousand burials, many rich in bronze and iron objects. These finds were so important that the whole Early Iron Age culture of central Europe is named after Hallstatt. A great landslide in the mid-4th century BCE ended the ancient mining.

name: Sivagalai
dateLabel: c. 1200–700 BCE (rice from a burial urn); a claim of iron at 3345 BCE is disputed
evidenceNote: A 2025 Tamil Nadu report dated iron here to 3345 BCE from charcoal, but rice from an urn with iron gave about 1155 BCE, and scholars question the early dates.
summary: An Iron Age urn-burial site near Adichanallur in Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, excavated by the state's archaeology department. In January 2025 its report 'Antiquity of Iron' announced radiocarbon and luminescence dates of 3345–2953 BCE for layers with iron objects, which would make it the oldest iron-working anywhere. Rice from an intact burial urn holding iron tools dated to about 1155 BCE, and scholars have pointed to disturbed layers and mixed samples, so the claim is not accepted as proven.

sources.title: Free Press Journal (23 Jan 2025): Tamil Nadu report dates iron to 3345 BCE

name: Teouma
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the burials are dated by radiocarbon and by the Lapita pottery buried with them.
summary: Teouma, near Teouma Bay on Éfaté in Vanuatu, holds the oldest known cemetery in the Pacific Islands, found in 2003. It contained burials of dozens of early Lapita people, about 3,000 years old. Many skulls had been removed after death and some replaced by cone-shell rings, showing elaborate funeral customs. Fragments of red, intricately decorated Lapita pottery were placed with the dead. Isotope tests on 17 individuals suggest that four of them grew up elsewhere and arrived as migrants, which helps show how people moved between islands.

name: Hastinapur
dateLabel: Painted Grey Ware town c. 1100–800 BCE (Lal; 2021–22 dig: from c. 1500 BCE); occupied into medieval times
evidenceNote: The mound is excavated and dated by pottery and radiocarbon; its link to the Kuru capital of the Mahabharata comes from tradition, not proof.
summary: A mound on the old bank of the Ganga in Meerut district, Uttar Pradesh, traditionally the capital of the Kuru kings in the Mahabharata and holy to Jains. B. B. Lal's excavations in 1950–52 found a Painted Grey Ware village of the early Iron Age, dated about 1100–800 BCE, ended by a Ganga flood, with later early-historic towns above. Lal linked that flood to the Mahabharata's story of a Ganga flood under King Nichakshu, a link many historians treat as tradition, not dated history.

name: Cuicuilco
evidenceNote: No writing existed here; the town is dated by radiocarbon and by the lava of the Xitle volcano that buried it.
summary: Possibly the oldest town in the Valley of Mexico, on the southern shore of the old Lake Texcoco in what is now Mexico City. Its best-known building is a large round, stepped pyramid begun a few centuries BCE. The settlement was destroyed when the nearby Xitle volcano erupted, some time between 245 and 315 CE, covering the area in lava. It was roughly contemporary with the Olmecs and may have had contact with them.

image.caption: The round pyramid of Cuicuilco (wide-angle view)

name: Tikal (early phase)
dateLabel: first farmers c. 1000 BCE; major building from c. 400 BCE; abandoned c. 900 CE
evidenceNote: Tikal's kings recorded their names and dates in Maya hieroglyphs, readable from the 3rd century CE onward, alongside excavation.
summary: A great Maya city in the rainforest of northern Guatemala, probably called Yax Mutal. Farmers lived here by about 1000 BCE, and major pyramids and platforms were going up by 400–300 BCE. In 378 CE a war leader linked to distant Teotihuacan arrived and the king Chak Tok Ich'aak died the same day, after which a new dynasty ruled. Its tallest temples date from after 500 CE. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Great Plaza of Tikal with Temple I, built centuries later in the Late Classic

name: Đông Sơn
evidenceNote: The Đông Sơn people left no writing of their own; the site is dated by archaeology, and Chinese texts describe the region only from outside.
summary: Đông Sơn is a village on the Ma River in Thanh Hóa Province, Vietnam, where bronze objects were first excavated in 1924. It gave its name to the Đông Sơn culture of the Red River and neighbouring valleys. Its people grew rice, kept water buffalo and pigs, sailed dugout canoes and were expert bronze casters. Their great bronze drums, cast with scenes of boats, warriors, houses and birds, were traded across Southeast Asia and southern China. The culture is often linked with the Lạc Việt, ancestors of the Vietnamese.

name: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa dolmens
dateLabel: c. 1000–300 BCE (Bronze Age; Gochang group c. 7th century BCE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the dolmens are dated by the Bronze Age objects found with them, so their dates are approximate.
summary: Korea has some 40 percent of all the world's dolmens, stone grave markers made of a huge capstone resting on smaller stones. Three clusters were listed by UNESCO in 2000. Gochang has 442 recorded dolmens, believed built around the 7th century BCE. Hwasun has dolmens beside the quarries that supplied their stones, and Ganghwa Island has large table-type dolmens, the most famous at Bugeun-ri. They were built by Bronze Age farming communities, and the largest capstones weigh well over 100 tonnes, which shows how many people leaders could gather.

image.caption: Table-type dolmen at Bugeun-ri, Ganghwa Island

sources.title: Wikipedia: Gochang, Hwasun and Ganghwa Dolmen Sites

name: Adichanallur
evidenceNote: Dated by radiocarbon (one set gives 905–696 BCE); claims of much older dates and of writing on the urns remain debated.
summary: A huge urn-burial ground on the Tamirabarani river in Thoothukudi district, Tamil Nadu, first dug in 1876 and by Alexander Rea in 1899–1905. Large pottery urns held human bones together with iron weapons and tools, bronze vessels and ornaments, and gold diadems. Excavations from 2004 found about 169 more urns, and radiocarbon dates put the burials in the early first millennium BCE. It is one of the key sites of the Iron Age of the far south, near the later Pandya port of Korkai.

image.caption: Burial urns in an excavation trench

name: Taxila
evidenceNote: Named by the grammarian Panini, by Greek writers who came with Alexander, and in inscriptions; its three city sites are excavated.
summary: A city of ancient Gandhara near Rawalpindi, Pakistan, at the meeting of routes from India, Central Asia and Iran. Its three cities, the Bhir Mound (from about the 6th century BCE), Sirkap (laid out by Indo-Greek kings) and Sirsukh (founded by the Kushans), together with Buddhist stupas and monasteries such as Dharmarajika, span about a thousand years. Its king submitted to Alexander in 326 BCE, and it was famous for learning. The Huns devastated it in the 5th century CE.

image.caption: The Dharmarajika stupa

name: Lapita type site (Site 13, Foué)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the settlement and its pottery were dated by radiocarbon after the 1952 excavation.
summary: The Lapita culture is named after Site 13 on the Foué peninsula of Grande Terre, New Caledonia, excavated in 1952 by Edward W. Gifford and Richard Shutler Jr. The name came from mishearing a local Haveke word meaning 'the place where one digs'. The site's finely decorated pottery, stamped with toothed tools in geometric patterns, was dated to about 800 BCE. More than 200 Lapita sites are now known from the Bismarck Archipelago to Samoa, and this pottery style became the marker for the first settlers of the remote Pacific.

name: Anuradhapura
dateLabel: settled c. 900 BCE; capital from the 4th century BCE to the 10th century CE; sacred city today
evidenceNote: Described in the Sri Lankan chronicles and in hundreds of inscriptions; excavations show settlement from about 900 BCE.
summary: The first great capital of Sri Lanka, on the Malwathu Oya in the island's dry north. Excavations show an Iron Age village from about 900 BCE; the chronicle Mahavamsa says King Pandukabhaya made it a capital in the 4th century BCE. It became a centre of Theravada Buddhism, with giant brick stupas such as the Ruwanwelisaya, the sacred Bodhi tree grown from a cutting of the Buddha's tree, and great irrigation reservoirs. It was sacked by the Cholas in 993 CE but remains a pilgrimage city.

image.caption: The Ruwanwelisaya stupa (2nd century BCE, restored in modern times)

name: Manunggul Cave (Tabon Caves)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the burial jar is dated by radiocarbon on material from the cave.
summary: Manunggul Cave is one of the Tabon Caves at Lipuun Point in Palawan, Philippines, a cave complex used for burials over thousands of years and explored in 1962–1966. Its most famous find is the Manunggul Jar, a secondary-burial jar dated to about 890–710 BCE. Its lid carries two figures in a boat, thought to show a soul being ferried to the afterlife, a common idea among Austronesian seafaring peoples. The jar is a National Cultural Treasure of the Philippines and is shown at the National Museum of Anthropology in Manila.

image.caption: The Manunggul Jar, National Museum of Anthropology, Manila

name: Nukuleka
dateLabel: founded c. 888 BCE; occupied for about 250 years
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the founding is dated very precisely by uranium-thorium dates on coral tools.
summary: Nukuleka, a fishing village on the northeast coast of Tongatapu in Tonga, is argued to be the first settlement in Polynesia. Excavations led by David Burley found Lapita pottery, and uranium-thorium dating of coral files used as abrading tools placed the founding at 2838 ± 8 years before present, about 888 BCE, with the settlement developing over the following 250 years. Archaeologists see it as a founder colony from which Polynesian culture developed. Some Tongan and Samoan scholars dispute the 'cradle of Polynesia' label.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE 7(11)

name: Songguk-ri
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the village is dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles from excavations since 1975.
summary: Songguk-ri, in Buyeo County, South Korea, is a large Middle and Late Mumun village and the type site for Middle Mumun culture in southern Korea. Excavations from 1975 found round pit-houses, a wooden palisade and ditches, and a stone-cist burial with a bronze dagger and large tubular greenstone beads, among the first bronzes found in South Korea. Analysis of plant remains shows that rice-paddy farming supported the village. Songguk-ri helped archaeologists recognise the growth of ranked societies in Korea in the first millennium BCE.

name: Carthage
dateLabel: founded c. 814 BCE (traditional date); destroyed 146 BCE; Roman city to 698 CE
evidenceNote: Greek and Roman writers describe the city; its founding date of 814 BCE comes from later tradition rather than from excavation.
summary: A city on the coast of Tunisia founded by Phoenician settlers from Tyre, traditionally in 814 BCE. It grew into the capital of a trading empire across the western Mediterranean and fought Rome in the three Punic Wars, including Hannibal's invasion of Italy. Rome destroyed it in 146 BCE; Julius Caesar founded a new city on the site, which became one of the largest in the Roman West until its destruction in 698 CE. Traces of its circular naval harbour survive. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Paracas cemeteries (Cerro Colorado)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the burials are dated by radiocarbon and by pottery and textile styles; the location here is approximate.
summary: Cemeteries on Cerro Colorado, a hill on the desert Paracas Peninsula on Peru's south coast, excavated by Julio Tello from the 1920s. The Cavernas are shaft tombs reused over centuries; sometimes heads of the dead were taken out for rituals and later reburied. The Wari Kayan necropolis held hundreds of burials of seated bodies wrapped in many layers of finely woven cloth. Their embroidered mantles are considered some of the finest textiles of the ancient Andes.

name: Matara
dateLabel: c. 8th century BCE – 7th century CE (approximate; pre-Aksumite to Aksumite)
evidenceNote: The town is known from excavation and from the Hawulti obelisk, which carries the oldest known inscription in the Geʽez script.
summary: An ancient town near Senafe in southern Eritrea, an important centre of the Dʿmt kingdom and later of Aksum, a few kilometres south of Senafe. Its most famous monument is the Hawulti, a pre-Aksumite or early Aksumite stone obelisk whose inscription is the oldest known example of the Geʽez script, still used today by Ethiopian and Eritrean churches. The Hawulti was toppled and damaged by Ethiopian troops during the Eritrean–Ethiopian War and has since been repaired by the National Museum of Eritrea.

image.caption: The Hawulti obelisk at Matara (Balaw Kalaw)

name: Meroë
dateLabel: c. 800 BCE – 350 CE; royal pyramids c. 300 BCE – 350 CE
evidenceNote: Meroitic inscriptions can be read aloud but are still not fully understood; Egyptian, Greek and Roman texts also describe Meroë.
summary: The capital of the Kingdom of Kush beside the Nile north of Khartoum in Sudan, from about 590 BCE to the 4th century CE. More than 200 steep-sided Nubian pyramids stand in its cemeteries, built for kings and queens from about 300 BCE. The city was a centre of iron-working and trade between Africa and the Mediterranean, and its rulers included powerful queens called kandake. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Pyramids of the Kushite royal cemetery at Meroë

name: Hire Benakal
evidenceNote: No writing; dated by the style of the tombs and finds and by comparison with dated megalithic sites.
summary: The largest megalithic cemetery in South India, on a rocky range of seven hills near Gangavati in Koppal district, Karnataka. About 400 tombs stand here, many of them dolmens: box-like chambers of huge stone slabs with a capstone, some with a round 'porthole' in one side, plus menhirs and stone circles. They date from the change from the Neolithic to the Iron Age, roughly 800–200 BCE. Painted rock shelters nearby show animals and people.

image.caption: Dolmens on the hillside

name: Olympia
evidenceNote: Greek inscriptions, victor lists and writers record the sanctuary and its Games, alongside excavations since the 1870s.
summary: Olympia, in the western Peloponnese, was a great sanctuary of the god Zeus and the home of the ancient Olympic Games. By tradition the first Games were held in 776 BCE, and they took place every four years for more than a thousand years. Athletes from all over the Greek world competed, which helped Greeks feel they were one people. The site had temples, treasuries, a stadium and training grounds. The Games ended in the 390s CE under the Christian emperor Theodosius I and later inspired the modern Olympic Games.

name: Great Dam of Marib
evidenceNote: Sabaean and Himyarite inscriptions record its building and repairs; its final collapse is remembered in the Qur'an.
summary: An ancient earth-and-stone dam across Wadi Adhanah near Marib in Yemen, first built in the 8th century BCE and enlarged many times. By catching the sudden floods it watered about 100 km² of fields that fed the Sabaean kingdom, famous for its incense trade. Its stone sluices still stand. After repeated breaches it finally failed in the late 6th century CE. The Marib monuments became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2023.

image.caption: Ruins of the ancient Marib Dam sluice works

name: Biskupin
dateLabel: built c. 747–722 BCE; lived in into the 6th century BCE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; tree rings in the oak timbers show when the trees were cut, and radiocarbon dates the later use.
summary: Biskupin in north-central Poland was a fortified wooden town on a marshy island, built by people of the Lusatian culture. Tree-ring dating shows its oak logs were felled between 747 and 722 BCE. About a hundred log houses of the same size and plan stood in neat rows along streets paved with planks, all inside a timber rampart. A schoolteacher and his pupils found it in 1933. Parts of the town have been rebuilt as an open-air museum.

image.caption: Reconstructed gate and rampart at Biskupin

name: Yeha (Great Temple)
evidenceNote: Inscriptions in the South Arabian script name kings of a state called Dʿmt; the temple's date comes from comparing its style with dated South Arabian buildings.
summary: A town in Tigray, northern Ethiopia, that was probably the capital of the pre-Aksumite kingdom of Dʿmt. Its Great Temple, a tall roofless tower of finely fitted stone blocks, was built in the Sabaean style of South Arabia (Yemen) around 700 BCE and still stands. Its inscriptions and design show close ties with South Arabia across the Red Sea. Nearby are the ruined Grat Beal Gebri complex and rock-cut shaft tombs, and a monastery and church stand beside the temple today.

name: Heuneburg
evidenceNote: The Celts here left no writing; excavation tells its story, and the idea that it was the town of Pyrene mentioned by the Greek writer Herodotus is only a possibility.
summary: The Heuneburg is a hillfort above the Danube in southern Germany and one of the most important early Celtic centres of the Hallstatt period. Around 600 BCE its builders replaced a timber wall with a whitewashed mudbrick wall on stone foundations, a Mediterranean technique unknown elsewhere north of the Alps. Valuable imported goods show trade with the Mediterranean world. Large burial mounds and an outer town surround it. It has been called the oldest city north of the Alps.

name: El Mirador
dateLabel: main city c. 600 BCE – 150 CE (later reoccupied)
evidenceNote: Dated mainly by radiocarbon and pottery; very few inscriptions survive from its peak.
summary: A huge Preclassic Maya city deep in the forest of northern Petén, Guatemala, linked to neighbouring towns by raised stone causeways. Its La Danta pyramid rises about 72 metres above the forest floor and, counting its giant platform, is one of the largest ancient structures in the world by volume. El Mirador flourished from the 6th century BCE, peaked from the 3rd century BCE, and was abandoned around 150 CE, centuries before Classic cities such as Tikal reached their height; it was partly reoccupied in the Late Classic. Reaching it still takes a long hike or a helicopter.

image.caption: The La Danta pyramid rising above the forest at El Mirador

name: Taruga
dateLabel: c. 600–200 BCE (iron smelting c. 4th–3rd century BCE)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the furnaces and terracottas are dated by radiocarbon from Bernard Fagg's 1960s excavations.
summary: A Nok culture site about 60 km southeast of Abuja in central Nigeria. Excavations in the 1960s found terracotta figures together with iron-smelting furnaces and slag dated to about the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, among the earliest evidence of iron working south of the Sahara. Whether West Africans learned iron smelting from North Africa or invented it themselves, building on copper smelting, is still debated.

name: Pompeii
evidenceNote: Pliny the Younger wrote an eyewitness account of the eruption, and thousands of inscriptions and graffiti survive on its walls.
summary: Pompeii was a wealthy Roman town of 10,000 to 20,000 people near Naples. In 79 CE the eruption of Mount Vesuvius buried it, with nearby Herculaneum, under metres of ash and pumice. Because it was sealed so quickly, excavators have found streets, shops, bakeries, houses with wall paintings, and even the shapes of people and animals left as hollows in the ash. Excavations began in the 18th century, and the town gives an unmatched snapshot of everyday Roman life.

name: Pataliputra (Kumhrar)
evidenceNote: Described by the Greek envoy Megasthenes and in Indian texts; the remains at Kumhrar were excavated from 1912.
summary: Remains of ancient Pataliputra, capital of Magadha and of the Maurya and Gupta empires, excavated at Kumhrar in modern Patna, Bihar. The town began as a fort built by Ajatashatru by the Ganga; under Chandragupta Maurya and Ashoka it became one of the largest cities in the world, visited and described by the Greek envoy Megasthenes. Excavators found a hall of 80 polished sandstone pillars of the Mauryan period and four phases of occupation from about 600 BCE to 600 CE.

image.caption: Excavated brick ruins at Kumhrar

name: Keezhadi
dateLabel: 6th century BCE–3rd century CE (radiocarbon); excavator proposes 8th century BCE; ASI questions this
evidenceNote: The town is real and radiocarbon-dated, but how early it began, and whether its inscribed potsherds are as old as the oldest dates, are contested.
summary: An early town on the Vaigai river near Madurai, Tamil Nadu, found in 2014 and excavated by the Archaeological Survey of India and then the Tamil Nadu archaeology department. Finds include ivory and terracotta dice, figurines, iron tools, punch-marked coins and potsherds scratched with Tamil-Brahmi names. Tamil Nadu reports radiocarbon dates from the 6th century BCE. The excavator, Amarnath Ramakrishna, argues for the 8th century BCE; in 2025 the ASI asked him to justify this. Some archaeologists doubt the inscribed sherds come from the earliest layers.

sources.title: Scroll.in (23 May 2025): ASI asks Amarnath Ramakrishna to rework his Keeladi report

name: Merv
evidenceNote: Named as Margu in Darius the Great's Behistun inscription (c. 515 BCE) and by later writers; its walled cities are excavated.
summary: A great oasis city of the Murghab delta in Turkmenistan. The first walled city, Erk Kala, was founded in the 6th century BCE as the Achaemenid Persians took over Margiana. The Seleucid king Antiochus I rebuilt it as Antiochia Margiana (today's Gyaur Kala), and Parthians, Kushans and Sasanians later ruled it; Buddhist stupas stood here. In the Middle Ages it became one of the largest cities in the world. Its overlapping walled cities form a World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Great Kyz Kala, a later (6th–7th century CE) building at Merv

name: Behistun inscription
evidenceNote: It is itself a written source, carved for Darius the Great in three languages.
summary: A huge relief and inscription carved high on a cliff at Mount Behistun near Kermanshah in western Iran, on the orders of Darius the Great after he seized the Persian throne in 522 BCE. It tells his version of how he defeated rebels, in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. Like the Rosetta Stone for Egyptian, its three matching texts let scholars in the 19th century decipher cuneiform writing. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Darius the Great's relief and inscription at Behistun

name: Persepolis
evidenceNote: Royal inscriptions on the buildings and thousands of administrative tablets document its construction.
summary: The ceremonial capital of the Persian (Achaemenid) Empire on the plain of Marvdasht in southern Iran, begun by Darius the Great around 518 BCE. On a great stone terrace stood audience halls with forests of columns. Staircase reliefs show delegations from across the empire bringing gifts to the king. Alexander the Great captured it in 330 BCE, and soon after the palaces burned. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Palace of Darius (Tachara) at Persepolis

name: Monte Albán
evidenceNote: Zapotec carvings with glyphs and dates survive here from early on, but the script is only partly understood; most knowledge comes from excavation.
summary: The capital of the Zapotec state, founded around 500 BCE on a flattened ridgetop 400 metres above the Valley of Oaxaca, Mexico. Its great plaza is lined with pyramids, platforms and a ballcourt. Its earliest carvings, the so-called Danzantes ('dancers'), show naked men, probably slain captives, and some carry early Zapotec glyphs. By about 100 BCE – 200 CE it ruled much of the Oaxaca region. It declined after about 750 CE. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The west side platform at Monte Albán

name: Nazca Lines
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the lines are dated by the pottery left beside them and by radiocarbon; their purpose is still debated.
summary: Giant designs scraped into the desert floor of southern Peru by moving dark stones to expose lighter ground beneath. Hundreds of straight lines, triangles and spirals cross the plain, with a total length of more than 1,300 km, along with figures such as a monkey, a hummingbird and a spider that are best seen from the air. Early ones were made by the Paracas people, most by the Nazca. Drones keep revealing new figures. Scholars still debate what they were for. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Monkey figure of the Nazca Lines, seen from the air

name: Kodumanal
evidenceNote: Named Kodumanam in the Sangam poems of the Patirruppattu, and its potsherds carry Tamil-Brahmi names; its dates rest on a few radiocarbon samples.
summary: An ancient craft town on the Noyyal river in Erode district, Tamil Nadu, called Kodumanam in Sangam poetry. Excavations found furnaces for iron and high-carbon steel, workshops cutting beads of carnelian, lapis lazuli, sapphire and quartz, megalithic burials and many potsherds with Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions. It lay on the trade route between the west-coast port of Muziris and Kaveripattinam on the east coast, part of the Indo-Roman trade network.

name: Acropolis of Athens (Parthenon)
evidenceNote: Athenian inscriptions and ancient writers record its building, as well as excavation and the surviving temples.
summary: The Acropolis is the rocky hill at the centre of Athens. In the 5th century BCE, after the Greeks defeated the Persian invasions, the Athenians rebuilt it with marble temples. The Parthenon, a temple to the goddess Athena, was begun in 447 BCE and finished in 438 BCE, with its sculptures completed by 432 BCE. It also served as a treasury. Later it became a church and then a mosque, until a Venetian bomb exploded gunpowder stored inside in 1687.

image.caption: The Parthenon on the Acropolis of Athens

name: Tollund Man (find site)
evidenceNote: No writing existed in Iron Age Denmark; the body was found in 1950 and dated by radiocarbon.
summary: In 1950 peat cutters near Silkeborg in Denmark found a man's body so well preserved that they thought he was a recent murder victim. He had died between about 405 and 384 BCE, in the Pre-Roman Iron Age. The acid, oxygen-poor bog had preserved his skin and face. A rope around his neck shows he was hanged, but nobody knows whether he was sacrificed or executed. He is one of the best known of northern Europe's many bog bodies.

name: San Bartolo
evidenceNote: Its painted texts of about 300–200 BCE are the earliest known Maya writing; they can be dated but most signs cannot yet be read.
summary: A small Maya site in the Petén forest of Guatemala, northeast of Tikal. In 2001, inside the base of a pyramid, a team led by William Saturno found a room with brilliantly painted murals of about 100 BCE showing Maya creation myths, the Maize God and a king, among the oldest Maya murals known. Fragments of painted plaster from about 300–200 BCE carry the earliest known Maya hieroglyphic writing, proving the script was in use centuries before the Classic period.

name: Cổ Loa Citadel
evidenceNote: The ramparts are dated by excavation and radiocarbon; the story that King An Dương Vương built them comes from much later legends and chronicles.
summary: Cổ Loa, about 17 km north of central Hanoi, is a huge fortified city with three spiralling rings of earthen ramparts and moats; the outer wall runs about 8 km and still stands up to 12 metres high. Excavations dated part of the inner rampart to around 400–350 BCE, and Đông Sơn pottery and a 72 kg bronze drum show a local society built it before Han Chinese rule. Vietnamese tradition credits King An Dương Vương of Âu Lạc and tells of a golden turtle that helped him, but these accounts were written down much later.

name: Yoshinogari
evidenceNote: The village is dated by pottery and radiocarbon; Chinese chronicles describe Japan's chiefdoms of this time, but none names Yoshinogari.
summary: Yoshinogari, in Saga Prefecture on Kyushu, is the largest and best-known Yayoi settlement in Japan. Radiocarbon dates suggest its first Yayoi phase began before 400 BCE. In the late Yayoi period it was surrounded by a deep V-shaped outer moat about 2.5 km long, enclosing some 40 hectares, with wooden fences, earth ramparts and watchtowers. Inside were raised-floor storehouses, storage pits, ritual areas and burials, with finds of pottery, bronze, iron and wood. Much of it is now a reconstructed historical park.

image.caption: Reconstructed buildings and watchtowers at Yoshinogari

name: Petra
dateLabel: c. 4th century BCE – 7th century CE; Treasury 1st century CE
evidenceNote: Nabataean inscriptions and Greek and Roman writers describe the city.
summary: The 'Rose City' of the Nabataeans, carved into red sandstone cliffs in southern Jordan. It grew rich as a hub of the incense trade and became the capital of the Nabataean kingdom. Its builders cut grand tomb facades such as the Treasury (Al-Khazneh) straight into the rock, and channels and cisterns stored scarce water. Rome annexed it in 106 CE; it declined after an earthquake in 363 CE. It is a UNESCO site.

image.caption: The Treasury (Al-Khazneh) at Petra lit by candles

name: Great Serpent Mound
dateLabel: built c. 300 BCE (Adena) or c. 1000 CE (Fort Ancient) — disputed
evidenceNote: Radiocarbon tests in 2014 and 2019 pointed to the Adena people about 300 BCE, but other archaeologists argue it was built by the Fort Ancient culture about 1,000 years later.
summary: A low earthen effigy of a snake about 411 metres long and 1 metre high, winding along a ridge above Ohio Brush Creek in southern Ohio, its head ending in an oval. It is the largest known serpent effigy in the world. Who built it, and when, is still argued: Adena people around 300 BCE, with later repairs, or the Fort Ancient culture around 1000 CE. The ridge sits on the edge of an unusual crater, possibly made by an asteroid impact about 300 million years ago.

image.caption: The coils of the Great Serpent Mound

name: Pattanam
evidenceNote: The excavated port is real, but whether it is Muziris, the famous Roman pepper port, is debated; some place Muziris at nearby Kodungallur.
summary: A buried port town near North Paravur in Kerala, excavated by the Kerala Council for Historical Research. It yielded a wharf, a dugout canoe, teak mooring posts and thousands of finds: Roman amphorae and glass, West Asian and Chinese pottery, beads and coins, mostly from about the 3rd century BCE to the 5th century CE. Its excavators identify it with Muziris, the great pepper port of Roman texts and Tamil poems. Other scholars argue Muziris lay at Kodungallur, where no comparable excavation has been made.

name: Ai-Khanoum
evidenceNote: Greek inscriptions found in the city, including Delphic maxims, date and describe it; its ancient name is unknown.
summary: A Greek city on the Amu Darya (Oxus) in northern Afghanistan, probably founded by a Seleucid governor around 300–285 BCE and a centre of the Greco-Bactrian kingdom. French excavations from 1964 uncovered a palace, a gymnasium, a theatre for about 6,000 people, temples and Greek inscriptions, including moral maxims copied from Delphi. It shows Greek culture flourishing in the heart of Asia. Saka invaders captured it around 145 BCE, and in recent decades the site has been badly looted.

name: Dujiangyan
dateLabel: built c. 256 BCE; still in use
evidenceNote: Chinese historical texts record the project and its builder, Li Bing, and the works themselves survive and still operate.
summary: Dujiangyan, on the Min River in Sichuan, is an irrigation and flood-control system built around 256 BCE by the state of Qin under its governor Li Bing. Instead of a dam, it divides the river and sends part of it through a channel about 20 metres wide cut through a mountain to the Chengdu Plain; the rock was cracked by heating it with fire and cooling it with water. It made the plain one of China's richest farming regions and helped Qin unify China. More than 2,200 years later it still irrigates over 5,300 square km. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

image.caption: The Dujiangyan irrigation works on the Min River

name: Grave Creek Mound
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the mound is dated by radiocarbon and by the Adena-style objects buried in it.
summary: One of the largest cone-shaped burial mounds in North America, about 19 metres high and 73 metres across, in Moundsville, West Virginia, on the Ohio River. People of the Adena culture moved more than 60,000 tonnes of earth to build it, about 250–150 BCE, over burials. Amateur diggers tunnelled into it in 1838, finding skeletons with beads, sea shells and copper bracelets, but destroying much evidence. It is the largest surviving Adena mound and now has a museum.

image.caption: Grave Creek Mound in Moundsville, West Virginia

name: Djenné-Djenno
evidenceNote: No writing survives from the site; it is dated by radiocarbon from excavations by Roderick and Susan McIntosh from 1977.
summary: The mound of 'old Djenné', 3 km from the modern town in the Inner Niger Delta of Mali. Settled around 250 BCE by people who grew African rice, kept animals and fished, it grew into an occupation mound of about 33 hectares, up to 6 metres high, linked to long-distance trade. It proved that towns and trade networks arose in West Africa on their own, before traders crossed the Sahara. It was abandoned around 1400. Part of the Old Towns of Djenné World Heritage Site.

name: Sanchi
evidenceNote: Hundreds of donor inscriptions on the railings and gateways, and an Ashokan edict, record who built and paid for it.
summary: A hilltop group of Buddhist monuments near Vidisha in Madhya Pradesh. The Great Stupa was begun by Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE as a brick dome over relics of the Buddha; it was later enlarged in stone and given a railing and four carved gateways (toranas) in the 1st century BCE, covered with stories from the Buddha's lives. Temples and monasteries were added until the 12th century CE. It is one of the oldest stone structures in India.

image.caption: East gateway of the Great Stupa

name: Sarnath
evidenceNote: Ashoka's pillar inscription, later inscriptions and accounts of Chinese pilgrims describe the site.
summary: The deer park near Varanasi where, by Buddhist tradition, the Buddha gave his first sermon. Ashoka raised a polished sandstone pillar here around 250 BCE, crowned by four lions back to back; this Lion Capital is now the State Emblem of India. Stupas, including the great Dhamek Stupa, and monasteries were built over the next 1,400 years, until the site was sacked in 1194. It was added to the World Heritage List in July 2026.

image.caption: Monastery ruins with the Dhamek Stupa behind

sources.title: Free Press Journal (July 2026): Sarnath added to UNESCO World Heritage List

name: Junagadh rock inscriptions (Girnar)
dateLabel: Ashoka c. 250 BCE; Rudradaman c. 150 CE; Skandagupta c. 456 CE
evidenceNote: The boulder itself is the written record: three dated royal inscriptions cut into it over 700 years.
summary: A large granite boulder at the foot of Mount Girnar, near Junagadh in Gujarat, carved with three royal inscriptions. The oldest is a set of fourteen of Ashoka's Major Rock Edicts, in Brahmi script, about moral rule. Around 150 CE the Western Satrap Rudradaman added one of the earliest long Sanskrit inscriptions, describing the repair of the Sudarshana reservoir first built under the Mauryas. A third, of the Gupta king Skandagupta, records repairs to the same dam. It is now sheltered by a building.

image.caption: The inscribed boulder inside its shelter

sources.title: Wikipedia: Junagadh rock inscription of Rudradaman

name: Amaravati Stupa
dateLabel: 3rd century BCE–c. 250 CE; known as a centre until the 14th century
evidenceNote: Inscriptions on its sculptures name donors and kings, and later texts mention it; the stupa itself is reduced to its base.
summary: A great Buddhist stupa beside the Krishna river in Andhra Pradesh, near the ancient city of Dharanikota. Built in phases from the 3rd century BCE to about 250 CE, under Satavahana and later rulers, it was faced with finely carved limestone slabs, some showing the stupa itself. Its style influenced Buddhist art in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. Neglected after Buddhism declined, it was buried under rubble until Colin Mackenzie surveyed it in 1816; many reliefs are now in Chennai, Amaravati and the British Museum.

image.caption: Carved drum slab showing a stupa (British Museum)

name: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang and the Terracotta Army
evidenceNote: The historian Sima Qian described the building of the tomb about a century later, and the army itself was found by excavation in 1974.
summary: Near Xi'an lies the burial mound of Qin Shi Huang, the first emperor of a unified China. Work began in 246 BCE when he became king of Qin, and the historian Sima Qian wrote that 700,000 conscripts laboured on it. In 1974 farmers digging a well found the Terracotta Army buried about 1.5 km away: three pits estimated to hold more than 8,000 life-size clay soldiers, 130 chariots and hundreds of horses, each face individually finished. They were buried with the emperor in 210–209 BCE. The central tomb has never been opened. UNESCO listed the site in 1987.

image.caption: Pit 1 of the Terracotta Army, Lintong, Xi'an

sources.title: Wikipedia: Mausoleum of Qin Shi Huang

name: Lumbini pillar of Ashoka
evidenceNote: Its Brahmi inscription states that Ashoka came here twenty years after his coronation because the Buddha was born here.
summary: A sandstone pillar in Lumbini, southern Nepal, raised by the emperor Ashoka when he visited the birthplace of the Buddha. Its short inscription in Prakrit says the king worshipped here 'because the Buddha Shakyamuni was born here' and made the village of Lumbini free of taxes, paying only an eighth share of its produce. The pillar was found in 1896, guided by the accounts of the Chinese pilgrims Faxian and Xuanzang, and the inscription helped confirm where the Buddha was born. Lumbini is a World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The pillar during its excavation in 1896

name: Lauriya Nandangarh
dateLabel: pillar c. 243–236 BCE (dating of Ashoka's reign varies)
evidenceNote: The pillar carries six of Ashoka's Pillar Edicts in Brahmi, cut late in his reign.
summary: A village in West Champaran, Bihar, with one of the best-preserved pillars of Ashoka: a single polished sandstone shaft crowned by a seated lion. It carries six of Ashoka's Pillar Edicts on moral conduct and was probably one of a line of pillars along the royal road from Pataliputra towards Nepal. Nearby rise the large brick stupa mound of Nandangarh and rows of earthen burial mounds, partly excavated in the 19th and 20th centuries.

image.caption: The Ashokan pillar with its lion capital

name: Beikthano
evidenceNote: Beikthano is dated by radiocarbon on its walls and buildings; the later Pyu cities left inscriptions, but few written records survive from Beikthano itself.
summary: Beikthano, near Taungdwingyi in Myanmar's dry zone, is one of the earliest walled cities of the Pyu, a people of the Irrawaddy valley. Its name means 'Vishnu city'. Excavations found brick walls about six metres thick, radiocarbon dated between about 180 BCE and 610 CE, along with buildings, pottery and human burials in a landscape of irrigated fields. Its earliest remains date to around 200 BCE to 100 CE, making it one of the oldest cities in Southeast Asia. With Halin and Sri Ksetra it forms the Pyu Ancient Cities World Heritage Site, listed in 2014.

name: Arikamedu
evidenceNote: Probably the port Poduke named in the Periplus and by Ptolemy; Roman pottery and coins date its trade.
summary: A riverside trading port near Pondicherry on the Coromandel coast. Mortimer Wheeler's excavation in 1945 found Roman amphorae, red Arretine tableware and lamps, and he called it an Indo-Roman trading station. Later work by Vimala Begley showed the port was busy from the 2nd century BCE to the 7th or 8th century CE and was a major maker of glass and stone beads traded across the Indian Ocean. It is generally identified with the 'Poduke' of Greek and Roman geographers.

image.caption: Terracotta child with a bird, 1st–2nd century CE

name: Ajanta Caves (early caves)
dateLabel: early caves c. 2nd century BCE–1st century CE; second phase c. 460–480 CE
evidenceNote: Donor inscriptions in the caves, some naming Vakataka rulers, help date the two phases.
summary: About thirty Buddhist halls and monasteries cut into a horseshoe-shaped cliff in Maharashtra. The first group, including the prayer halls (chaityas) Caves 9 and 10, was carved in the 2nd–1st centuries BCE and still holds some of the oldest surviving Indian paintings. After centuries of quiet, a burst of work in about 460–480 CE under the Vakataka king Harishena added the famous painted caves. Forgotten for centuries, they were found by a British tiger-hunting party in 1819.

image.caption: The horseshoe cliff of the Ajanta caves

name: Mawangdui
evidenceNote: Seals and silk manuscripts buried in the tombs name their owners, so the tombs are known from their own writing as well as excavation.
summary: Mawangdui, in Changsha, Hunan, held three Western Han tombs of the family of Li Cang, chancellor of the Changsha Kingdom, who died in 186 BCE; his son was buried in 168 BCE. Excavated in 1972–1974, they were sealed so well that Li Cang's wife, Xin Zhui (Lady Dai), was found with her body remarkably preserved, together with silk clothes, lacquerware and food. A painted silk banner shows the heavens, earth and underworld. Tomb 3 held a trove of manuscripts on silk, including a copy of the Daodejing, military, medical and astronomical texts, and early maps.

name: Karla Caves
evidenceNote: Donor inscriptions in the caves name merchants, monks, Satavahana and Western Satrap rulers.
summary: Buddhist rock-cut caves near Lonavala in Maharashtra, on an old trade route from the Arabian Sea ports into the Deccan. Their Great Chaitya (Cave 8), cut in the 1st century CE, is the largest and best-preserved prayer hall of its age: a long vaulted nave that still keeps its original wooden roof ribs, rows of pillars with sculpted elephants, and a stupa at the end. Inscriptions record gifts from merchants, several Yavana (Greek) donors and kings.

image.caption: Inside the Great Chaitya

name: Óc Eo
evidenceNote: Chinese records describe the kingdom of Funan, and seals and objects at Óc Eo carry short Sanskrit inscriptions, alongside excavated remains.
summary: Óc Eo, in An Giang Province in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, was a large port of the kingdom of Funan, known from Chinese records. Found by aerial photography and first excavated by Louis Malleret in 1942, it covers about 450 hectares and was linked by canals to the sea and to Angkor Borei, 68 km away. Finds include Roman gold medallions of the emperor Antoninus Pius, gold jewellery, silver coins minted in Funan and Hindu statues such as a Vishnu. Óc Eo shows how the Mekong Delta joined a trade network reaching from Rome to China.

name: Bharhut
dateLabel: railings c. 125–100 BCE (some argue 1st century CE); later abandoned
evidenceNote: Each relief panel is labelled in Brahmi script, and donor inscriptions name the patrons; the date of the carvings is debated.
summary: A Buddhist stupa in Satna district, Madhya Pradesh, whose carved stone railing and gateway are among the earliest Indian sculpture. Uniquely, many panels are labelled in Brahmi, naming the Jataka tales, the Buddha's life scenes and spirits such as yakshas. The stupa may have been begun under Ashoka; most of the carving is usually dated about 125–100 BCE. Alexander Cunningham found the ruin in 1873, and most surviving pieces are in the Indian Museum, Kolkata.

image.caption: Cunningham's reconstruction of the stupa and its railing

name: Teotihuacan
dateLabel: c. 100 BCE – 550 CE (centre burned); declined to c. 650 CE
evidenceNote: The city left signs and murals but no readable texts; its history comes from excavation and from Maya inscriptions that mention it.
summary: The greatest city of the ancient Americas, about 40 km northeast of modern Mexico City. Its Avenue of the Dead runs past the Pyramid of the Sun and the Pyramid of the Moon, among the largest pyramids of the Americas. At its height in the first half of the 1st millennium CE perhaps 100,000 people lived in its multi-family compounds, decorated with bright murals. Its influence reached Maya cities such as Tikal. Around 550 CE its centre was burned. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Pyramid of the Sun, with the Pyramid of the Moon behind, at Teotihuacan

name: Hegra (Mada'in Salih)
dateLabel: 1st century BCE – Roman period; tombs mainly 1st century CE
evidenceNote: Many tomb facades carry dated Nabataean inscriptions naming their owners.
summary: The second city of the Nabataean kingdom after Petra, near Al-'Ula in northwestern Saudi Arabia. More than 110 well-preserved tombs are carved into sandstone outcrops, many with inscriptions giving their owner and date. The settlement grew mainly in the 1st century CE under King Aretas IV and passed to Rome in 106 CE. Dry air and no later rebuilding have kept it in excellent condition. It was Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO site, in 2008.

name: Tillya Tepe
dateLabel: graves c. 1st century BCE–1st century CE
evidenceNote: Known from the 1978 excavation; coins buried in the graves, including a Roman coin of Tiberius, date them.
summary: A mound near Sheberghan in northern Afghanistan where Viktor Sarianidi's Soviet–Afghan team found six graves in 1978, of five women and one man, with about 20,600 objects of gold, silver, turquoise and ivory. The 'Bactrian Gold' mixes Greek, Iranian, Indian and steppe styles, such as a folding gold crown of trees and birds. The dead were probably nomad nobles of the time the Kushans rose. The hoard went missing during the Afghan wars and resurfaced safely in 2003.

image.caption: Gold crown from Tomb VI

name: Aksum (stelae fields)
dateLabel: capital from c. 1st century BCE–1st century CE; great stelae c. 300–400 CE
evidenceNote: Aksum is 'written': its kings left inscriptions in Geʽez, Sabaic and Greek and issued coins, and Greek and Roman writers describe it.
summary: The capital of the Kingdom of Aksum in northern Ethiopia, a trading power that issued its own coins and adopted Christianity under King Ezana in the 4th century. Its royal cemetery holds giant granite stelae carved like multi-storey towers with false doors and windows, marking tombs. The Great Stele, 33 metres long, probably fell as it was being raised. The 24-metre Obelisk of Axum, taken to Rome by Fascist Italy in 1937, was returned to Ethiopia in 2005. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Stelae in the main stelae field at Aksum
image.credit: Adam Jones from Kelowna, BC, Canada

name: Sarmizegetusa Regia
evidenceNote: Roman writers describe the Dacian wars, and a vessel found here carries the name of King Decebalus.
summary: Sarmizegetusa Regia, high in the Orăștie Mountains of Romania, was the capital and holy centre of the Dacians. King Burebista moved his capital here near the end of his reign in the 1st century BCE, and it reached its height under King Decebalus. Its fortress of stone walls stood beside a sacred area of temples, including a circular sanctuary. The Romans under Emperor Trajan defeated the Dacians in two wars (101–106 CE), took the city, put a garrison in it and tore down much of its fortress.

name: Hathigumpha inscription, Udayagiri
dateLabel: c. 1st century BCE (from the style of its letters)
evidenceNote: A seventeen-line royal inscription in Prakrit; it is undated, so it is placed by the shape of its Brahmi letters.
summary: A seventeen-line Prakrit inscription carved in Brahmi above the 'Elephant Cave' in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar, Odisha. It was cut for Kharavela, a Jain king of Kalinga, and lists his deeds year by year: repairing gates and a canal, campaigns into the north and the south, and gifts to Jain monks, for whom the nearby caves of Udayagiri and Khandagiri were carved. It is the main source on Kalinga after Ashoka's conquest. Its letter shapes place it around the 1st century BCE.

image.caption: The inscription of Kharavela

name: Cahuachi
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the site is dated by radiocarbon and by Nazca pottery styles.
summary: The main ceremonial centre of the Nazca culture, beside the Nazca River and overlooking some of the Nazca Lines. It has more than 40 adobe-topped mounds spread over about 1.5 km². Archaeologists once thought it was the capital of a Nazca state, but few people lived here permanently. It seems instead to have been a pilgrimage centre whose population swelled before and during great ceremonies. Many of its mounds are natural hills reshaped with adobe, and looting of its cemeteries is a serious problem.

image.caption: Adobe mounds at Cahuachi in the Nazca valley

name: Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks (Newark)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the earthworks are dated by radiocarbon and by Hopewell objects found in nearby mounds.
summary: The Newark Earthworks in Ohio, with a Great Circle about 360 metres across and an Octagon joined to a circle, are the largest geometric earthen enclosures in the world. The Octagon is aligned to the 18.6-year cycle of moonrises. Built by people of the Hopewell tradition, they belong with Mound City, Hopewell Mound Group and other Ohio sites to the Hopewell Ceremonial Earthworks, inscribed in 2023 as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. They were places for gatherings, feasts, funerals and ceremonies.

image.caption: The wall and inner ditch of the Great Circle at Newark

sources.title: US National Park Service: Hopewell Culture National Historical Park

name: Sipán (Huaca Rajada)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the tombs are dated by radiocarbon and by Moche pottery and metalwork styles.
summary: Eroded adobe pyramids in the Lambayeque valley of northern Peru, where tomb looters tunnelled in and struck gold in February 1987. Archaeologists Walter Alva and Susana Meneses then excavated royal tombs from 1987 to 1990, above all that of the 'Lord of Sipán', a Moche ruler buried with a spectacular treasure of gold, silver and gilded copper ornaments. It was one of the richest burials ever found in the Americas, and its finds are now in the Royal Tombs of Sipán Museum in Lambayeque.

image.caption: Reconstruction of the Lord of Sipán's tomb at Huaca Rajada

name: Pont du Gard
dateLabel: 1st century CE; used perhaps until the 6th century
evidenceNote: It is a Roman engineering work dated by archaeology and building style; Roman records of the aqueduct do not give an exact year.
summary: The Pont du Gard is a three-tiered Roman aqueduct bridge over the river Gardon in southern France. Built in the 1st century CE, it carried water about 50 kilometres to the Roman city of Nemausus (Nîmes). The whole channel drops only a tiny amount over its length, showing how precisely Roman engineers worked. It may have carried water until the 6th century, but it was poorly maintained after the 4th. It is one of the best-preserved Roman aqueduct bridges.

image.caption: The Pont du Gard over the river Gardon

name: Takht-i-Bahi
evidenceNote: An inscription naming the Indo-Parthian king Gondophares was found at the site; the monastery is excavated.
summary: A Buddhist monastery on a ridge near Mardan in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan, in the heart of ancient Gandhara. Founded in the 1st century CE and used until the 7th, it has courts of stupas, monks' cells, assembly halls and a meditation area, all of local stone, and was once full of Gandharan sculpture mixing Greek and Indian styles. Its hilltop setting saved it from later destruction, and UNESCO calls it exceptionally well preserved.

image.caption: The monastery ruins on their ridge

name: Colosseum
evidenceNote: Roman writers and inscriptions record its building and the shows held in it.
summary: The Colosseum in Rome is the largest amphitheatre ever built. Emperor Vespasian began it around 72 CE and his son Titus opened it in 80 CE. Built of travertine stone, concrete and tuff, it could hold an estimated 50,000 to 80,000 spectators, who watched gladiator fights, animal hunts and public executions. Gladiator fights are last mentioned in the 5th century, and animal hunts continued until at least 523 CE. Earthquakes and stone robbers later damaged it, but much still stands.

image.caption: The Colosseum in Rome

name: Huacas del Sol y de la Luna
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the temples are dated by radiocarbon and by Moche pottery styles.
summary: Two huge adobe brick pyramids near Trujillo on Peru's north coast, the heart of the southern Moche state. The Huaca del Sol was built in eight stages by 450 CE from over 130 million adobe bricks, the largest adobe structure in the pre-Columbian Americas; makers' marks suggest more than a hundred communities supplied bricks. In the 17th century Spanish colonists diverted the Moche River against it to hunt for treasure. The smaller, better-preserved Huaca de la Luna has brightly painted reliefs of a fanged god.

image.caption: Painted relief of a fanged deity at the Huaca de la Luna

name: Tiwanaku (early city)
dateLabel: founded c. 100 CE (dates debated); peak c. 500–1000; abandoned c. 1050 CE
evidenceNote: No writing existed; older claims of 1500 BCE or earlier are rejected, and a study of reliable radiocarbon dates puts its founding around 110 CE.
summary: A ceremonial city near the southern end of Lake Titicaca in western Bolivia, about 70 km from La Paz. It grew from about the 2nd century CE and by 500 CE was the leading power of the Titicaca basin, with the terraced Akapana platform, the Kalasasaya enclosure and the precisely cut stone platforms of Pumapunku. Perhaps 10,000–20,000 people lived there around 800 CE. The famous Gate of the Sun belongs to its later centuries. A UNESCO World Heritage Site.

image.caption: The Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku, from the city's later centuries

name: Hadrian's Wall
dateLabel: begun 122 CE; Roman rule ended c. 410 CE
evidenceNote: Roman inscriptions, writing tablets and histories record the wall and its soldiers.
summary: Hadrian's Wall was begun in 122 CE on the orders of Emperor Hadrian. It ran about 117 kilometres across northern England, from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth, marking the northern frontier of Roman Britain. Soldiers lived in large forts, smaller milecastles and turrets along it, and its gates may have been customs posts; when fully manned, it may have held almost 10,000 troops. Roman rule in Britain ended around 410 CE, though some forts stayed in use into the 5th century.

name: Pantheon, Rome
evidenceNote: Roman texts and the inscription on its front record it, although Hadrian copied the older builder Agrippa's name onto it, so its exact date is uncertain.
summary: The Pantheon in Rome is a temple to all the gods, rebuilt under Emperor Hadrian and probably dedicated around 126 CE on the site of an earlier temple by Agrippa. A porch of granite columns leads into a round hall covered by a concrete dome with an open hole, the oculus, at the top. Almost two thousand years later it is still the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome. Since 609 CE it has been a church, which is one reason it survives so well.

name: Hashihaka Kofun
evidenceNote: The mound is real, but it has never been fully excavated, its date is argued, and whether it is the tomb of Queen Himiko is unproven.
summary: Hashihaka, in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture, is one of the earliest large keyhole-shaped burial mounds in Japan, often taken as the start of the Kofun period. Some archaeologists date it to the mid to late 3rd century, close to the death of Queen Himiko of Yamatai, whom Chinese chronicles say died around 248, and suggest it may be her tomb. Others date it to the 4th century. The Imperial Household Agency manages it as the tomb of a legendary princess, Yamato Totohi Momoso, and allows only limited survey, so the debate remains open.

name: Kutai yūpa inscriptions
dateLabel: second half of the 4th century CE
evidenceNote: The stone pillars carry Sanskrit inscriptions naming King Mulavarman, dated by the style of their script.
summary: Near Muara Kaman on the Mahakam River in East Kalimantan, Borneo, seven stone pillars called yūpa were found carved with Sanskrit verses in an early Pallava script. They praise Mulavarman, a king of Kutai, his father and grandfather, and record lavish gifts to Brahmin priests after sacrifices. Dated by their script to the second half of the 4th century CE, they are the oldest known inscriptions in Indonesia and show an Indian-influenced kingdom there before 400 CE. The pillars are now in the National Museum in Jakarta.

name: Mogao Caves
evidenceNote: Inscriptions and later texts record the caves' founding and patrons, and the Library Cave held tens of thousands of manuscripts.
summary: The Mogao Caves, about 25 km southeast of Dunhuang in Gansu, are a system of some 500 Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff on the Silk Road. The first caves were dug in 366 CE, and new caves were added for about a thousand years, until the 14th century. Their wall paintings and clay statues show how Buddhist art travelled from India and Central Asia into China. In 1900 a walled-up 'Library Cave' was found, full of manuscripts, including the Diamond Sutra of 868, the earliest dated printed book. UNESCO listed the caves in 1987.

name: Iron pillar of Delhi
dateLabel: c. 400 CE (reign of Chandragupta II, c. 375–415 CE)
evidenceNote: Its Sanskrit inscription honours a king Chandra, generally identified as the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II.
summary: A pillar of wrought iron about 7 metres tall and over six tonnes, now standing in the Qutb complex in Delhi. Its Sanskrit inscription praises a king Chandra, identified as Chandragupta II of the Gupta Empire, and calls it a standard of the god Vishnu. It probably first stood elsewhere, perhaps at Udayagiri, and was moved to Delhi in the 11th century. It has barely rusted in 1,600 years because of a thin protective layer formed on its high-phosphorus iron.

image.caption: The iron pillar in the Qutb complex
image.credit: Mark A. Wilson (The College of Wooster)

name: Theodosian Walls of Constantinople
dateLabel: c. 405–413 CE; defended the city until 1453
evidenceNote: Roman law codes and an inscription found in 1993 record the building of the walls.
summary: The Theodosian Walls protected the land side of Constantinople (today Istanbul), the new capital of the Roman Empire. Building began around 405 CE and was finished in 413 under Emperor Theodosius II. Most scholars think a second, outer wall and a moat were added after an earthquake in 447. They were the last great fortification system of the ancient world. For a thousand years they held off attackers, until the Ottoman Turks took the city in 1453. Long stretches still stand.

name: Gwanggaeto Stele
evidenceNote: The stele is itself a contemporary written record, carved with about 1,800 Chinese characters.
summary: The Gwanggaeto Stele stands near the tomb of King Gwanggaeto the Great of Goguryeo in Ji'an, Jilin, on the Yalu River, then Goguryeo's capital. Raised in 414 CE by his son, King Jangsu, it is a single block of granite about 6.39 metres tall carved with around 1,775–1,802 characters. The text tells Goguryeo's founding myth and lists the king's campaigns against Baekje, the Wa from Japan and others. Rediscovered around 1876, it is a key source for early Korean history, though one passage about the Wa is hotly debated. It is part of a UNESCO site.

image.caption: The Gwanggaeto Stele in its pavilion at Ji'an

name: Nalanda
evidenceNote: Seals, inscriptions and accounts by Chinese pilgrims such as Xuanzang describe the monastery; coins link its founding to Kumaragupta I.
summary: A great Buddhist monastery and centre of learning in Bihar, near Rajgir, founded around 427 CE under the Gupta emperor Kumaragupta I. Monks and students from across Asia studied philosophy, logic, grammar and medicine in its brick monasteries and temples, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang spent years here in the 7th century. Often called one of the world's first residential universities, it declined after attacks around 1200 and faded by about 1400. Its excavated ruins are a World Heritage Site.

image.caption: Temple No. 3 at Nalanda

name: Daisenryō Kofun
evidenceNote: The giant mound is real, but it has never been excavated, and its traditional owner, Emperor Nintoku, cannot be confirmed.
summary: Daisenryō, in Sakai near Osaka, is the largest kofun in Japan: a keyhole-shaped mound about 500 metres long inside triple moats, with the whole tomb area about 840 metres long. It is thought to have been built over some 20 years in the mid-5th century. The Imperial Household Agency treats it as the tomb of Emperor Nintoku and keeps it closed, so its identity cannot be tested. It belongs to the Mozu Kofun Group, part of the Mozu-Furuichi UNESCO site listed in 2019, which shows the power of the Yamato kings.

name: Yungang Grottoes
evidenceNote: Chinese histories record that the Northern Wei court sponsored the caves, and inscriptions survive in them.
summary: The Yungang Grottoes, 16 km west of Datong in Shanxi, are Buddhist cave temples cut into a sandstone cliff under the Northern Wei dynasty, whose capital was then nearby Pingcheng. Carving began around 460 CE with five huge Buddha caves, continued with imperial support until the court moved to Luoyang in 494, and ended in 525. There are 53 major caves and about 51,000 niches with Buddha statues. They blend Indian and Central Asian Buddhist art with Chinese traditions. UNESCO listed them in 2001.

image.caption: Colossal seated Buddha of Cave 20, Yungang Grottoes

name: Sigiriya
dateLabel: royal citadel 477–495 CE; monastery until the 14th century
evidenceNote: The Sri Lankan chronicle Culavamsa describes King Kashyapa's citadel, and visitors' verses scratched on the 'Mirror Wall' survive.
summary: A granite rock about 180 metres high in central Sri Lanka, made a fortress-palace by King Kashyapa I (477–495 CE). He built a palace on the summit, reached through a gateway shaped as a giant lion, of which the paws remain, and laid out water gardens below. Painted women survive in a sheltered pocket of the rock, and the polished 'Mirror Wall' carries verses left by later visitors. After his defeat it returned to use as a Buddhist monastery, as it had been since the 3rd century BCE.

image.caption: The Lion Rock above the water gardens

name: Lydenburg Heads site
evidenceNote: No writing existed; charcoal found with the heads is radiocarbon dated to about 1,410 years ago; the point marks the town of Lydenburg.
summary: A farm near Lydenburg in Mpumalanga, South Africa, where a boy found pieces of seven hollow terracotta heads, among the oldest known Iron Age artworks south of the equator. Found with pottery, iron and copper beads and bones, and dated to about 500 CE, they belong to early farming communities who brought iron, crops and cattle to the region, part of the spread of Bantu-speaking peoples. They are now in the Iziko South African Museum, Cape Town.

name: Nan Madol
dateLabel: megalithic building from c. 1180–1200 CE; capital until c. 1628 (later than this atlas's ancient period)
evidenceNote: Pohnpei had no writing; the city is dated by radiocarbon and uranium-thorium dates on coral, and its history is also told in Pohnpeian oral tradition.
summary: Nan Madol, off the island of Pohnpei in Micronesia, is a city of small artificial islets built in a lagoon and linked by a network of canals. Its walls are made of stacked columns of black basalt, some weighing several tonnes. Islet building began by the 8th or 9th century, and the megalithic architecture from about 1180–1200 CE, much later than the other ancient sites here. It was the ceremonial and political seat of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled Pohnpei until about 1628. UNESCO listed it in 2016.

name: Rapa Nui moai
dateLabel: carved mostly c. 1250–1500 CE (later than this atlas's ancient period)
evidenceNote: The Rapa Nui had no writing when the statues were made (the rongorongo script is later and unread); dates come from radiocarbon.
summary: The moai are giant stone figures carved by the Rapa Nui people of Easter Island, mostly between 1250 and 1500 CE, after Polynesians settled the island around 1200. Almost all of the more than 900 known statues were cut from volcanic tuff at the Rano Raraku quarry, where nearly 400 remain, many buried to the shoulders. Hundreds were moved across the island and set on stone platforms called ahu, facing inland. By the 1860s all standing moai had been toppled. Rapa Nui National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Wairau Bar
dateLabel: settled c. 1288–1300 CE (later than this atlas's ancient period)
evidenceNote: No writing existed; the settlement is dated by radiocarbon, and DNA and isotope studies of the burials add detail.
summary: Wairau Bar, a gravel bar at the mouth of the Wairau River in Marlborough, New Zealand, is one of the earliest known settlements in the country. Explorers from East Polynesia arrived here about 1280, and refined radiocarbon dating puts the village at about 1288–1300 CE. Graves held whole moa eggs used as water carriers, necklaces of moa bone, argillite adzes and other ornaments of East Polynesian style, showing that the first settlers hunted these giant flightless birds. Studies of the skeletons and their DNA give a rare picture of the founding population.

name: Atlantis (legend)
dateLabel: Plato (c. 360 BCE) set it c. 9600 BCE
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found. Atlantis comes only from two dialogues written by the philosopher Plato, and classicists agree it is a made-up story.
summary: Atlantis is the island empire in Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias, written around 360 BCE. Plato says it lay 'beyond the Pillars of Heracles' (the Strait of Gibraltar) and sank 9,000 years before the time of the Athenian lawmaker Solon, after losing a war against an idealised early Athens. Scholars read it as a moral tale about pride and power. Some suggest Plato borrowed ideas from real events such as the Thera eruption, but no ruins have ever been found. The point here only marks where Plato placed it.

name: Tower of Babel (legend)
dateLabel: Legend; no date can be given
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found for the tower of the Genesis story; many scholars think Babylon's real Etemenanki ziggurat may have inspired it, but that link is a hypothesis.
summary: In chapter 11 of the Book of Genesis, people who all speak one language build a city and a tower reaching to the sky in the land of Shinar (southern Mesopotamia), and God scatters them by confusing their speech. It is an origin story for the world's many languages, not a historical record. Because the Hebrew name Babel means Babylon, modern scholars most often link the tale to the city's huge ziggurat, Etemenanki. The marker is placed there only to show that link.

name: Kumari Kandam (legendary)
evidenceNote: Not proven: no archaeological evidence has been found, and geology shows no sunken continent in the Indian Ocean.
summary: A lost land said to lie south of Kanyakumari, swallowed by the sea with an ancient Tamil civilisation. Medieval commentaries tell of Pandya lands and the first two Tamil literary academies (Sangams) lost to the ocean; 19th-century European ideas of a sunken continent, 'Lemuria', were then joined to these stories by Tamil revivalists, who coined the name Kumari Kandam in the 1930s. Plate tectonics has disproved Lemuria, and no ruins have been found. The point here only marks where tradition places it.
